title: MetaShift: A Grounded Continual Benchmark Where the Improvement Procedure, Not the Task, Must Change
claim: Under shifts in the improvement regime (evaluator flakiness, feedback granularity, eval budget), systems with an editable improver recover at least twice as fast as fixed-improver systems. Under task-content shifts of matched difficulty (library-version API drift), they show no advantage. This crossover interaction separates 'the harness must change' from 'the improver must change'.
alt: If editable improvers show no advantage even under regime shifts, current self-referential loops do not actually adapt their procedure when it matters, which explains the low natural self-update rate as a capability gap and gives the field a benchmark to fail on. If they win equally under both shift types, improver editability is generic extra capacity rather than procedure learning. Both outcomes are publishable alongside the benchmark itself.
design: Benchmark built from real drift. (i) Task-content shift: code tasks pinned to real library versions with documented breaking changes (pandas 1->2, numpy 1->2, pydantic 1->2, sourced from changelogs, in the style of GitChameleon or VersiCode), so the right API changes but the improvement procedure need not. (ii) Regime shifts drawn from real CI practice: flaky tests at measured real-world flake rates (noise 0 -> 15%), a feedback-granularity shift (per-test logs -> pass/fail only -> aggregate scalar), and an eval-budget cut (200 -> 30 evals per generation). Each schedule runs 12 generations pre-shift and 12 post-shift. Systems, all in GodelLite: fixed improver; editable improver at the natural rate; editable improver with a meta gate. We also run ACE/GEPA-style prompt optimizers as external baselines. 4 shift types x 3 systems x 5 seeds = 60 runs, with Qwen3-32B and gpt-oss-120b. Budget is matched. Metrics: recovery time (generations until 90% of the pre-shift held-out score is regained), post-shift area under the curve, and IFR-style replay showing whether the post-shift improver is better than the pre-shift improver on frozen post-shift states. The primary preregistered test is the system x shift-type interaction on recovery time (mixed model). A manipulation check confirms that hand-designed regime-appropriate procedures (e.g., majority-vote re-evaluation under flakiness) beat the fixed improver, so the benchmark truly requires procedure change. Cost: about $1.1k.
law: n/a (dissociation claim: the recovery-time ratio fixed/editable is above 2 for regime shifts and about 1 for task shifts)
pilot: Two shifts only (flaky-test noise vs pandas API drift), fixed vs natural-editable, 3 seeds, 8+8 generations, plus the oracle-procedure manipulation check, about $55. Go if the oracle procedure beats the fixed improver by at least 5 points post flaky-shift (the shift is procedure-relevant) and the fixed improver loses at least 10 points post-shift. Kill if the fixed improver is unaffected by noise, which would mean the regime shift is too weak; in that case raise the flake rate or switch to the granularity shift.
closest: Delta-tau-Bench, Continual Learning Exam, 'Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?' and EmbodiedCLBench (shift tasks only); Flex-RSI 2611.08946 (shows feedback granularity matters but holds it static); VERSE 2610.02616 (49% non-reproducible validations, i.e. noise, but not shifted); Meta-Forgetting/IFR eIJH6HV9LZ (replay metric, reused). Delta: the first benchmark that shifts the improver-relevant regime using real drift sources and tests a preregistered crossover between task shift and procedure shift.

closestFound.overlap: Highest on metric and framing: a recovery-time-after-shift metric for a meta-level loop. check.reposition:
No paper found runs the preregistered crossover: an exogenous improvement-regime shift (flakiness, granularity, eval budget) vs a matched-difficulty task-content shift, crossed with a fixed vs editable improver. The design is open, but three risks make it medium-risk.

(1) Likely null result: SelfImprove-Bench and Improvement by Inheritance show improvers almost never self-edit at the natural rate. So 'editable at natural rate' will probably behave like 'fixed'. Make this the finding: edit-rate locked to shift onset is the primary measurement. Keep the meta-gated or forced-edit arm as the condition that can show the >2x effect, and say plainly that natural-rate editability fails to detect regime shifts.

(2) The manipulation check cuts both ways: BudgetAPO and PID-gating show a fixed but regime-adaptive hand-designed procedure handles noise and budget. Add a 'fixed adaptive' baseline (BudgetAPO or PID gate, majority-vote re-eval). Then claim only that editable improvers approach this oracle procedure under regime shift and not under task shift. Do not claim that editability is necessary.

(3) Metric novelty is gone: CMAS already has adaptation delay. Cite it and present recovery time as borrowed. Put the contribution in the dissociation and the real CI-sourced shift generators (flake rates from published flaky-test studies, version drift from changelogs).

Also cite RuHarness, RSIFlow and Flex-RSI as the static 'procedure must change' evidence that MetaShift turns into a controlled shift test. Watch Flex-RSI v2 and CMAS follow-ups for a mid-run granularity or noise shift. Move fast: get a preprint out by about Feb 2027.

judges.strongest: The preregistered crossover design (system x shift-type on recovery time) is the right way to separate 'the harness must change' from 'the improver must change'. The oracle-procedure manipulation check, real drift sources (changelog API breaks, flake rates from published studies) and IFR replay on frozen post-shift states make it a mechanistic test rather than another leaderboard. It speaks directly to the user's question of why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves, and it turns that question into a measurable failure.
judges.weakest: "Matched difficulty" between task shifts and regime shifts is not defined in any operational way, so the central crossover is confounded. Recovery time depends on drop size and on the pre-shift baseline, and regime shifts such as granularity loss or budget cuts may barely hurt a fixed improver (ceiling or floor effects). On top of that, natural-rate editability will almost certainly look the same as fixed (SelfImprove-Bench, Inheritance), so the headline >2x effect can only come from a meta-gated or forced arm. That arm then looks like a hand-designed procedure, and the BudgetAPO/PID-gate results already show a fixed adaptive procedure can do this job. At 5 seeds, with censored recovery times (some runs never recover within 12 generations), an interaction test is underpowered.
judges.mustFix: (1) Define matched difficulty operationally: calibrate every shift so the fixed improver's immediate post-shift drop is the same (e.g., 10±2 points), and report recovery normalized by drop size. (2) Always measure held-out score with a clean, full-granularity evaluator that is separate from the shifted improvement-loop signal; otherwise 'recovery' under flakiness is ill-defined. (3) Add a fixed-adaptive baseline (BudgetAPO or a PID gate with majority-vote re-eval) and a forced-edit-at-shift arm. Reframe the claim as 'editable improvers approach the oracle under regime shift and not under task shift', and make edit-rate locked to shift onset a primary preregistered outcome. (4) Analyze recovery with a survival/Cox model to handle censoring, and raise seeds to at least 8 on the two primary shifts, cutting the budget shift if needed. Do a power analysis using the pilot variance. (5) Spell out that the budget-cut condition breaks matched compute by design, and match total compute across systems inside each condition. (6) Cite CMAS for adaptation delay, and RuHarness, RSIFlow and Flex-RSI as static prior evidence. Release the shift generators as the reusable artifact.
judges.reviewerQuote: "The crossover framing is clever, and the manipulation check is more careful than most RSI work. But the authors never show that the task and regime shifts are of comparable severity, so the interaction may just reflect the size of the drop. The 'editable' advantage also comes almost entirely from a gated arm that looks a lot like the fixed adaptive procedures in BudgetAPO. With five seeds and censored recovery times, I am not convinced the interaction is real. Weak accept if the calibration and the adaptive baseline are added; otherwise borderline."

judges.strongest: The preregistered crossover is the right experiment. It sets an exogenous shift in the improvement regime (flakiness, feedback granularity, eval budget) against a task-content shift, crossed with fixed vs editable improvers. That turns the field's static claims that the procedure must change (RSIFlow, RuHarness, Flex-RSI) into a falsifiable test. It also speaks directly to the user's question of why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves. The edit-rate-locked-to-shift-onset measurement holds up even if the main effect turns out null.
judges.weakest: The two arms are not matched in difficulty, and the 'editable' arm will probably behave like the fixed one. Nothing defines what makes a pandas 1->2 drift equal in difficulty to 15% flake noise. If they are not matched, the crossover is confounded by shift magnitude. Natural-rate self-edits are known to be near zero (SelfImprove-Bench, Improvement by Inheritance), so natural-editable will likely match fixed. BudgetAPO and PID gating already show that a fixed but regime-adaptive procedure handles noise and budget. That leaves the strong claim ('editable recovers at least 2x faster') with little room to hold. The 'grounded in reality' framing is also thin. Real flake rates come from published studies, but the noise is still injected synthetically, and an aggregate-scalar granularity shift does not happen in real CI. Twelve post-shift generations with a 90% recovery threshold will give many censored, coarse recovery times, and 5 seeds of agentic runs is a small sample.
judges.mustFix: (1) Calibrate difficulty. Match the two shift types on the size of the fixed improver's post-shift drop (equal Δ in held-out score), and report the crossover conditional on that match. (2) Add a fixed-but-adaptive baseline (BudgetAPO, a PID gate, majority-vote re-eval) and a forced-edit or meta-gated arm. Reframe the claim from 'editability is necessary' to 'editable improvers approach the oracle procedure only under regime shift'. Report the natural-rate edit null as a primary finding. (3) Treat recovery time as censored: use survival or Cox models with at least 8 seeds, and use post-shift AUC as a co-primary metric. (4) Add a third base model, or at least one stronger model, so the null is not dismissed as 'the open models are too weak to self-edit'. (5) Cite CMAS for the recovery metric, and put the contribution in the dissociation plus the released shift generators. Preprint by about Feb 2027 to get ahead of Flex-RSI v2.
judges.reviewerQuote: A clean, well-motivated dissociation design. But the authors never establish that the task and regime shifts are of comparable magnitude, and the most likely result (natural-rate editable improvers act like fixed ones, and hand-designed adaptive procedures beat both) reduces the headline claim to a negative result about current models. I would raise my score if difficulty were matched explicitly and the fixed-adaptive baseline were included.

judges.strongest: The design tests a real question in the mentor's area. A system x shift-type crossover, run under one harness (GodelLite) with fixed and editable improvers, asks whether a Gödel-style loop changes its procedure when the procedure is what needs to change. Most self-improvement papers only assume this happens. Both shift generators come from real drift: flake rates from published studies, and API breaks taken from pandas, numpy and pydantic changelogs. Together they make a benchmark others can reuse even if the main hypothesis fails. The oracle-procedure manipulation check, and a pilot of about $55 with explicit go/kill thresholds, are the right instincts.
judges.weakest: The headline effect most likely does not exist in the form claimed, and the comparison between the two shift types is not well defined. (a) At the natural rate, editable improvers almost never self-edit (SelfImprove-Bench, Improvement by Inheritance), so 'natural-editable' will look the same as 'fixed'. The >2x result then rests on the meta-gated arm, and that arm is partly hand-designed. (b) 'Matched difficulty' between flaky tests and pandas drift has no operational definition. Without one, a reviewer will say the interaction comes from the size of each shift, not its type. (c) The fixed-adaptive procedures in BudgetAPO and PID-gating already handle noise and budget regimes. That weakens 'the improver must change' into 'some regime-aware procedure is needed'. (d) Lowering the eval budget from 200 to 30 removes information. No improver edit can restore it, so recovery to 90% of the pre-shift score may never happen in any arm. That produces censored, degenerate recovery-time data. (e) Twelve post-shift generations is too few to estimate a recovery-time ratio when the fixed arm often never recovers.
judges.mustFix: 1) Define matched difficulty as an equal post-shift drop for the fixed improver, calibrated in the pilot. Tune the flake rate and the drift severity until the two shift types give the same drop, then preregister those settings. 2) Add a fixed-adaptive baseline (BudgetAPO or PID gate with majority-vote re-evaluation). Restate the claim as: editable improvers close X% of the gap to the oracle procedure under regime shift and about 0% under task shift. 3) Make the edit rate locked to shift onset a co-primary measure, and use a forced-edit arm instead of only the meta gate, so the expected natural-rate null becomes a finding. 4) Use a survival model of recovery (Cox or censored regression), with censoring when a run never recovers. Do not treat the ratio as a raw point estimate. Extend to at least 20 post-shift generations, or drop the budget-cut shift. 5) Keep the granularity shift and the flaky shift as the headline regime shifts. Leave out budget or treat it separately, because it confounds procedure change with information loss. 6) Cite CMAS for the adaptation-delay metric. Present RuHarness, RSIFlow and Flex-RSI as the static evidence, and get a preprint out by February 2027, before Flex-RSI v2.
judges.reviewerQuote: The benchmark is useful, and the task-shift vs regime-shift framing is clever. But the claimed crossover comes from comparing two shift families whose sizes are not equated. The editable-improver advantage appears only in a gated arm whose gate the authors designed themselves, and a fixed noise-adaptive optimizer (BudgetAPO) matches it. As a result I cannot tell whether the result is 'self-referential procedure learning' or 'a well-chosen hand-built detector'. Weak accept if the fixed-adaptive comparison and a calibrated difficulty match are added.

title: Modularly Varying Goals for Meta-Harnesses: Editable Improvers Pay Only Under Real API Drift, as Evolvability Does in Biology
claim: Borrowing Kashtan and Alon's modularly-varying-goals result from evolutionary biology, the held-out advantage of an editable improver (L4) over a fixed improver (L3) is near zero or negative on static task streams. It becomes positive, and spontaneous improver-edit rates rise, when the stream switches among real library-version regimes on a schedule. The advantage peaks at intermediate switching periods.
alt: If L4 shows no advantage under drift either, then editable improvers do not acquire evolvability-like adaptive capacity even when the environment rewards it. The 'improve the improver' agenda would then be unsupported for continual settings, and constrained adaptive-scope or memory methods suffice. This is a strong negative, with a reusable, grounded continual benchmark as its by-product. If L4 wins equally under static and drift conditions, drift is not the moderator. That contradicts the biology analogy and localizes L4's value to static headroom, which is also informative given the Hyperagents and Inheritance dispute.
law: Evolvability analog: Adv_L4(P) ≈ a·(1/P)·(1 − e^{−P/τ}) − c. There is no advantage at P=∞ (no selection for adaptability) and none as P→1 (switching faster than the improver's adaptation time τ). The peak is at P* ≈ τ, which is measurable from L3 recovery curves. The prediction is that P* scales with improver adaptation time, so stronger optimizers should have a smaller P*.
pilot: Week 1, about $45 plus a modest GPU. Build a 2-regime mini-stream (pandas 1.5 ↔ 2.2, 60 tasks with hidden tests). Run L3 vs L4 × 3 lineages at P=3 and P=∞ for 9 epochs. Go if (i) the unadapted harness loses ≥15 points on each regime switch (real drift exists and is not trivially absorbed by the model), (ii) both arms recover partially within 3 epochs (the task is learnable), and (iii) L4 improver-edit rate at P=3 exceeds that at P=∞ by any margin, or the L4−L3 gap differs by more than 1 seed-SD between P conditions. Kill if model priors already handle both versions (switch drop under 5 points). If that happens, switch to less-memorized libraries such as polars or recent pydantic minors.
closest: Kashtan & Alon 2005 PNAS (modularly varying goals produce modularity and evolvability, but in biological networks, not LLM agents). CodeUpdateArena 2407.06249, GitChameleon 2411.05830 and VersiCode 2406.07411 (static version-aware evaluation, with no continual stream and no self-improvement loop). SelfImprove-Bench 2611.02797 and Hyperagents 2603.19461 (static tasks). EvoSpace MQoRwlss2y and DyScope MXINrso5QC (adapt scope, but with no drift manipulation). Governing Self-Improvement Across Timescales c3lHKtsSMq (cost of memory/refinement, with no editable improver or drift). Delta: drift rate is the experimental moderator of openness's value, the stream is a grounded continual benchmark built on real changelogs that structurally requires improver-level adaptation, and the law borrows its form from evolvability theory.

check.reposition:
I found no paper that varies the switching period P as a moderator of the editable-vs-fixed improver gap (L4 vs L3), or that tests an inverted-U or evolvability-style law for meta-harness openness. That core claim is open. The surroundings are crowded, though. 2610.25858 owns drifting streams × editable surface × Meta-Harness with P/S/I/F metrics. 2611.03219 owns forgetting under continual coding harness evolution. SkillShift owns real, dated library-change events with version-pinned execution. To survive:
(1) Make the headline the arm × P interaction and the P* ≈ τ prediction, measured out of sample: estimate τ from L3 recovery curves first, then predict where the peak lands for a second optimizer strength. Demote DriftStream to an enabling contribution. Cite SkillShift and GitChameleon as data sources and handle stale or removed-API tests explicitly.
(2) Adopt 2610.25858's blocked-stream protocol and P/S/I/F metrics so the work reads as a direct extension along the switching-rate axis. Add their Mix (interleaved) schedule as an extra P→0 point.
(3) Pre-empt the empty-arm risk that SelfImprove-Bench and Improvement by Inheritance raise. Pilot L4 at P=3 before committing. Report the improver-edit rate as a primary dose-response outcome over P, which is a novel finding even if held-out gains are small. Add a forced-improver-edit arm, so a null cannot be blamed on improvers that never self-edit.
(4) Derive the law from a simple model, for example a two-timescale tracking model or the Kashtan-Alon setup applied to edit-acceptance dynamics, rather than asserting the functional form. Check that the observed peak beats a monotone alternative with a model-comparison test.
(5) Pull in 2611.03219's conflict taxonomy (verification, workflow, budget) for coding improver-edit content, and separate genuine meta-level edits ('check installed version', 'consult changelog') from task-level patches.

judges.strongest: The idea manipulates one environmental variable, switching period P, as a moderator of the L4-vs-L3 gap. This turns the vague question "is a more open search space better?" into a testable interaction contrast. It also explains the Hyperagents vs Inheritance dispute as a property of the environment rather than of the method: static streams give no reason to edit the improver. The improver-edit rate measured as a dose-response over P speaks directly to the user's question of why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves. It is publishable even if held-out gains are small. The benchmark is grounded in real breaking changes and checked by version-pinned hidden tests.
judges.weakest:
The headline inverted-U law is underpowered and confounded.
(a) Four P values with 6 lineages each cannot tell an inverted-U from a monotone curve or a saturating one. The functional form is fitted after the fact, not derived.
(b) P is tangled up with other quantities: number of switches, regimes seen per lineage, and tokens L4 spends on meta-edits versus task work. "Matched tokens per epoch" does not match exposure to regime diversity.
(c) Qwen3.5-27B has very likely memorized pandas 2, NumPy 2 and pydantic v2. The drift may then be absorbed by the model's priors or by a single 'check the version' prompt line, which L3 and the memory arm can also learn. That would erase the L4-specific mechanism.
(d) The held-out 'future regime' (pandas 3.0 or a later NumPy) may also be in pretraining.
(e) The empty-arm risk is real: L4 may edit its improver almost never under every P.
(f) Writing and verifying about 300 new tasks across 5 libraries, plus Docker images, is a heavy load for one undergrad on top of 72+ lineage runs.
judges.mustFix:
1. Frame the work as a direct extension of 2610.25858. Adopt its blocked-stream protocol and its P/S/I/F metrics, add its Mix schedule as the P→0 point, and use at least 6 P values (including Mix, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, ∞). This is needed to fit an inverted-U against monotone and saturating alternatives, with pre-registered model comparison (AIC or Bayes factor).
2. Measure τ from L3 recovery curves first. Then predict P* out of sample for a second optimizer strength or model size, otherwise the 'law' is curve-fitting.
3. Control the exposure confound. Match the number of distinct regime-epochs and switch counts, or include them as covariates. Count improver-edit tokens against the L4 budget.
4. Add a forced-improver-edit arm and an 'L3 + version-check prompt' baseline. These show whether L4's advantage is more than one cheap meta-line that a fixed improver could also carry.
5. Pick less-memorized drift as a priority: polars, recent pydantic or FastAPI minors, or synthetic-but-realistic API forks with a memorization check. Use post-cutoff releases for the held-out regime.
6. Shrink new-task authoring to about 100 tasks by reusing GitChameleon, VersiCode and SkillShift items. Handle stale tests for removed APIs.

It is fitted on four P values with six seeds each, and P is confounded with exposure to regime diversity. On libraries the base model has memorized, I am not convinced the drift requires improver-level adaptation rather than one version-check line any fixed improver could learn. Show the predicted P* moving out of sample with optimizer strength, and I will raise my score."

judges.strongest: The moderator itself still looks open: no paper we found varies the switching period P as the variable that sets the editable-vs-fixed improver (L4 vs L3) gap. This turns the vague "is open search space better?" debate into a testable interaction, and the prediction that the peak P* tracks the improver's adaptation time τ can be checked out of sample. The design also puts real version-pinned API drift behind the user's "grounded continual learning" ask, and measuring improver-edit rate as a function of P is worth reporting even if held-out gains turn out small.
judges.weakest:
The mechanism mapping is loose. API drift is mostly a first-order problem: a fixed L3 improver can add "check the installed version" or "consult the changelog" steps to the task harness without ever editing itself. So drift may not select for improver-level change at all, and a null result would be uninterpretable. Kashtan-Alon predicts modular structure, not a self-editable optimizer. The law also has the same 1/P · (1−e^{−P/τ}) shape you would get from any lag model, and four P values cannot tell an inverted U from a monotone curve.

Feasibility is tight. The full grid is 2-3 arms × 4 P × 6 lineages, about 72 multi-epoch runs of a 27B model, plus Docker images and about 300 new hidden-test tasks. That is a lot for one undergrad on ≤$3k in 6 months. The design also uses a single model and leaves the stale-test hazard open.

The neighbours are crowded. 2610.25858 already owns drift streams × editable surface with P/S/I/F metrics, 2611.03219 owns forgetting under continual coding-harness evolution, and SkillShift owns real library-version drift with version-pinned execution. Model priors on the well-known pandas 2 and NumPy 2 changes could also absorb the drift.
judges.mustFix:
(1) Construct the drift so it actually requires an improver-level change. One way is regimes that differ in what feedback or verification signal is available (for example, changelog access or test visibility flipping), not just in API surface. Then show in the pilot that L3, editing only the task harness, cannot close the gap.
(2) Use at least 6 P values, including 2610.25858's Mix schedule as the P→0 point. Pre-register a model comparison of inverted-U against monotone and saturating alternatives. Derive the law from a two-timescale tracking model, with τ estimated from L3 recovery curves before the L4 runs.
(3) Add a forced-improver-edit arm and a second open model of a different strength to test the P* shift. Stay within budget by cutting lineages per cell to 4-5 and using smaller task sets.
(4) Pilot on less-memorized libraries from the start (polars, recent pydantic minors). Handle stale and removed-API tests explicitly.
(5) Present the work as an extension of 2610.25858 along the switching-rate axis: reuse its protocol and metrics, and cite SkillShift and GitChameleon as data sources rather than claiming the benchmark as the contribution.
judges.reviewerQuote: "The paper's interesting question is whether drift rate controls the value of an editable improver. But in this setup a fixed improver can absorb library-version drift by patching the task harness, so I am not convinced the environment ever selects for self-modification. With four switching periods and one model, the evolvability law reads as curve-fitting with a nice biological story."

judges.strongest: The core manipulation is clean and, as far as anyone has checked, nobody has done it: switching period P as a moderator of the editable-improver (L4) versus fixed-improver (L3) gap. It fits Gödel Agent directly. It also explains the "improver rarely edits itself" finding in SelfImprove-Bench and Improvement by Inheritance: static streams give no reward for adaptability. The improver-edit rate as a dose-response over P is a new behavioral measurement that can be published even if held-out gains are small.
judges.reviewerQuote: The question is good and the drift-as-moderator design is the right way to settle the 'improve the improver' debate. But the proposed functional form is monotone and cannot produce the peak the paper claims. The single-model, single-domain evidence does not support calling it a 'law'. With the law derived properly and an out-of-sample P* test, this would be a solid accept; as written, it is a borderline reject.

title: The Openness Optimum Moves: A Token-Matched Permission Ladder Shows Held-Out Gain Peaks at an Intermediate Editable Surface Whose Location Shifts With Optimizer Capability and Verifier Noise
claim: With the optimizer, budget and tasks held fixed and only the editable surface randomized, held-out gain is an inverted U over openness rungs L0-L5, and the peak rung moves to more open surfaces as optimizer capability and validation-set size grow (and to less open ones as evaluator noise grows).
alt: If gain rises monotonically to L4/L5 for every tier, the 'bitter lesson for scaffolds' holds even for open mid-size models, and OEO's crossover is a quirk of its two systems. That is publishable as the first randomized-surface refutation. If gain is flat across rungs once tokens are matched, the result extends the Mirage, TPE and token-matched evolution nulls to the openness axis: openness differences between published systems are mostly proposer and budget artifacts. That is an important negative for the field.
design: Shared testbed 'LadderLoop': a Meta-Harness-lite keep-if-better loop in which one config file sets which files the proposer may write. Rungs: L0 numeric slots/few-shot ids; L1 free system-prompt text; L2 a typed DSL of operators (retry, verify, decompose, memory-read); L3 full task-harness Python; L4 +the proposer/improver prompt and code; L5 +parent selection and archive logic. The evaluator always stays external and read-only. Optimizers span three capability tiers: Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-27B (local vLLM), and one cheap frontier-mini API model on a reduced grid. Tasks: (a) an exact-evaluator task (CO-Bench subset of 6 heuristics problems); (b) a noisy agentic task (tau2-bench retail or an AppWorld subset); (c) a far-transfer split, where the harness evolved on (b) is scored on a held-out domain. Each lineage gets 2M proposer+executor tokens (matched tokens, not iterations) and 5 seeds per cell. The noise axis is n_val ∈ {16, 64, 256}, crossed only for the 27B tier. Controls: the same rung with a random/blind proposer (NAS-style, which separates space quality from proposer); a matched-token test-time-scaling baseline (best-of-k with the unedited harness); and the unedited baseline. The metric is held-out gain on a sealed test split never used for selection. The analysis fits a hierarchical model with rung as an ordinal factor and pre-registers a peak-location test, bootstrapping the argmax rung per tier/n_val and running a Jonckheere trend test on peak location versus capability and n_val. The law form is fit and compared with monotone and flat alternatives by held-out-cell prediction.
law: Pre-registered: Gain_heldout(O,B,n,σ) ≈ A(O)(1−e^{−B/B0(O)}) − c·σ·sqrt(2 ln N_eff(O,B)/n_val), with A saturating-increasing in O, B0 increasing in O, and N_eff the effective number of distinct accepted candidates (measured). It predicts an interior optimum O* with dO*/d(capability)>0, dO*/dn_val>0 and dO*/dσ<0. The model is fit on 2/3 of cells and validated on the remaining third.
pilot: Week 1, about $40 on local 27B plus API calls for the 4B smoke test. Run rungs L1, L3 and L4 × 3 seeds × 0.5M tokens on CO-Bench (2 problems) and the tau2 subset, at n_val=64. Go if (i) the held-out gain spread across rungs exceeds 2× the seed SD on at least one task, and (ii) L4 lineages make ≥1 accepted improver edit in ≥2/3 seeds when permitted (otherwise the rung is nominal-only and the design must lean on idea 2's forcing). Kill or reframe if all rungs fall within seed noise of the matched TTS baseline. In that case, pivot to the flat-null paper with the random-proposer decomposition as the main result.
closest: OEO 2608.09629 (capability crossover, but between two systems at a fixed surface, with no ladder, noise axis or random-proposer control). HarnessOpt-Bench 2608.06301 (breadth is an outcome, not a randomized treatment). SelfImprove-Bench 2611.02797 (compares ACE/AHE/Hyperagents, so system and surface are confounded). Harness Evolution as Learning 2609.36892 (U-shape in memory length L only). Mirage da1Czy7foS and Reachability oTYVUBHmbe (random search is competitive at a single surface). Delta: the first design where openness is the randomized treatment at a fixed optimizer and matched tokens, crossed with capability and n_val, and fit to a falsifiable functional form.

closestFound.title: RobustSGPO: Search-Space Control for Agent Harness Evolution (Sep 2026)
closestFound.summary: Uses a 3-rung permission ladder in the AgentX brainstorming workflow: alpha1 edits one agent, alpha2 edits any existing agent, alpha3 can also add or remove agents and change routing. Fixed-permission test scores are 3.85, 4.07 and 4.06, so the curve flattens or dips slightly at full openness. A periodic 1->2->3 schedule beats fixed maximum permission by 0.28. The paper separates the nominal, realized and effective edit spaces and reports results at matched 20M tokens.
closestFound.overlap: Highest. This is already a matched-budget permission ladder with held-out test and 5 seeds, and its result is roughly saturating, not monotone. It differs from the idea in four ways: one optimizer, one industrial workflow, 3 rungs (none touch the improver or the archive), and no capability axis, n_val/noise axis, random-proposer control or fitted law. A reviewer can cite it to say that 'more permission is not monotonically better' is already shown.

closestFound.title: EvoSpace: Co-Evolving the Harness and Edit Space for Memory-Grounded QA
closestFound.summary: Argues that a fixed edit space blocks needed updates, while opening every permissible edit at the start makes selection too hard. It progressively expands the edit space across components, scopes and operations, guided by diagnosis, and reports gains on LoCoMo with qwen3.6-flash and GPT-5.1.
closestFound.overlap: High on the motivation. It states the 'too closed vs too open' tension as its key insight and uses two optimizer models. It is a method paper, though: there is no randomized ladder, no peak-location test and no law, and the comparison is expanding vs fixed rather than a dose-response curve.

closestFound.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution (Nov 2026)
closestFound.summary: Runs AHE, HyperAgents, A-Evolve and GEPA on two harnesses: MiniSWE (source-editable) and Codex (outer-layer-only). It finds that reflection-centric methods' test reliability holds up on the source-editable harness but declines on the outer-only one, and that transfer depends on the editable surface.
closestFound.overlap: Medium. Editable surface is a factor here, but it is confounded with the harness itself (MiniSWE vs Codex) and has 2 levels. It uses one optimizer (GPT-5.4), and there is no ladder, no noise axis and no law. It supports the idea's premise that the surface matters.

closestFound.title: Where Does Harness-Optimization Value Live? Localized Gains and the Budget-Splitting Trap (HARNESSEVO)
closestFound.summary: Splits the harness into 4 slots with one reflective optimizer at iso-budget, using leave-one-in and leave-one-out attribution. Nearly all of the value sits in the reflection/control slot. Splitting the budget uniformly across slots drops each slot below the optimizer's 'effective search floor', and every slot freezes at its empty seed.
closestFound.overlap: Medium. It shows that widening the editable surface at a fixed budget can hurt, which is the B0(O)-increasing term in the proposed law. Its unit is slots, not an openness ladder, and it uses a single 7B model.

closestFound.title: RSI-Env (Nov 2026) and Evo-Bench (Aug 2026)
closestFound.summary: RSI-Env: in a fully open model+harness environment, stronger external improvers (GPT-5.6/GPT-6) are not consistently better than the 27B system improving itself, and they use the budget very differently. Evo-Bench: 9 evolver models of different capability on one fully open harness surface; gains scale with capability, and the paper reports early saturation and a tendency to make local prompt and filter edits.
closestFound.overlap: Medium-low. Both vary capability at a single (open) surface, so they cover the capability axis but not openness as a treatment. They are useful as evidence that the capability × openness interaction is non-trivial.

closestFound.title: Theory of Reliable Self-Evolution; Self-Evolving Agent Harness (continual PAC); Harness Evolution as Learning
closestFound.summary: These derive admission and generalization bounds of the form Δ̂ + sqrt(2 ln(KT/δ)/m) + 2η, and an approximation/estimation/optimization decomposition.
closestFound.overlap: The noise term in the proposed law (σ·sqrt(2 ln N_eff / n_val)) is essentially these existing bounds. The functional form will not read as new theory. The contribution has to be the empirical test, including measuring N_eff, and the location of the optimum.

check.reposition:
I found no paper that randomizes openness over 5 or more rungs at a fixed optimizer and matched tokens, crosses it with optimizer capability and n_val, and tests whether the peak moves. That still looks open. The headline claim is not: 'an intermediate surface beats the most open one' already has a single-optimizer instance in RobustSGPO (fixed α2≈α3>α1; scheduling beats fixed maximum permission), and EvoSpace states it as its key insight. To survive review:
(1) Make the headline the peak-SHIFT interaction (dO*/d capability > 0, dO*/d n_val > 0, dO*/dσ < 0), not the inverted U itself. Cite RobustSGPO, EvoSpace and HARNESSEVO as single-optimizer slices that the ladder generalizes.
(2) Frame the law as an empirical test of the existing PAC/admission bounds (2609.08175 eq. 9, 2610.18813, 2609.36892), in which N_eff(O) is measured. Do not present it as new theory. The new part is showing that A(O) and B0(O) make the bound predict where the optimum sits.
(3) Add an 'expanding/scheduled openness' arm (RobustSGPO 1→2→3 / EvoSpace-style). Test whether the fitted law predicts when and how fast expansion beats the best fixed rung. This turns closely related prior work into a prediction target.
(4) Keep the random/blind-proposer control and the L4/L5 rungs (improver and archive editable). No prior ladder includes them, and they connect to the SelfImprove-Bench / Improvement-by-Inheritance finding that improvers rarely edit themselves. Report the realized-vs-permitted edit distribution per rung, which RobustSGPO calls nominal vs realized vs effective space.
(5) Report pass@k and coverage alongside held-out mean (Elicitation-or-Expansion 2610.27889), and match on tokens (2610.23977), to head off the standard reviewer objections.

judges.strongest: The editable surface is the randomized treatment, with the optimizer and token budget held fixed. That breaks the system-vs-surface confound in OEO, SelfImprove-Bench and Beneath the Surface. The random/blind-proposer control at each rung separates how good the space is from how good the proposer is. The L4/L5 rungs, where the improver and the archive are editable, plus the realized-vs-permitted edit logging, speak directly to the user's question of why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves. The pre-registered peak-shift test and the held-out-cell law validation make the claim falsifiable in a way most work in this area is not.
judges.weakest: The headline is a peak-SHIFT interaction, and the design cannot detect it. An argmax over 6 ordinal rungs with 5 seeds is very unstable under bootstrap. A Jonckheere test on only 3 capability tiers (or 3 n_val levels) has almost no power. The capability axis is also confounded: Qwen 4B vs 27B vs a frontier-mini model differ in coding and tool-use skill, not on one 'capability' dimension. 'Openness' is not a scalar either. L2 (typed DSL) and L3 (free Python) differ in kind, so the 'ordinal rung' assumption, and with it the law's O, is a modeling choice that reviewers will attack. The full grid does not fit a solo undergrad's 6 months and $3k. Roughly 6 rungs x 3 tasks x 3 n_val x 5 seeds x 2M tokens comes to about 540M tokens for the 27B tier alone. Doubling for the random-proposer controls, then adding tau2's user simulator, the 4B tier, the frontier-mini grid and the proposed expansion arm, likely puts it beyond 1B tokens. The law's noise term is borrowed from existing PAC/admission bounds, and RobustSGPO already shows 'intermediate surface beats the most open one' at a single optimizer, so the inverted U by itself is not new.
judges.mustFix: (1) Run a simulation-based power analysis from the pilot variance before committing. If it shows the peak shift cannot be detected, collapse to 4 rungs (L1, L2/L3 merged or chosen, L4, L5) and test the interaction as a rung x tier contrast in the hierarchical model, not by bootstrapping argmax. (2) Replace or augment the ordinal rung with a measured openness covariate: N_eff, realized edit-space entropy, or the number of distinct accepted diffs. The law can then be fit on a continuous O and does not depend on the ladder's arbitrary spacing. (3) Make capability within one family (Qwen3.5 4B/9B/27B, or 27B with ablated reasoning budget) so it is not confounded with family. Treat the API tier as a single-cell sanity check. (4) Cut the grid to fit the budget. Use one exact task (CO-Bench) and one noisy task (tau2), and run far-transfer only on the best and worst rungs. Cross n_val only at 2 rungs. Run the expansion arm only at the 27B tier. Write a token and GPU-hour budget in the proposal. (5) Pre-commit the null framing: a flat result plus the random-proposer decomposition is a Datasets & Benchmarks fallback, not main track. Say so explicitly and release LadderLoop as the reusable artifact.
judges.reviewerQuote: The question is right and the random-proposer control is a real contribution. But the paper's central claim, that the optimum moves with capability and verifier noise, rests on an argmax across six rungs of uneven spacing, estimated from five seeds and three model sizes from different capability regimes. The inverted U itself is already in RobustSGPO. Unless the authors show they have the power to detect the shift, and that 'openness' is a measured quantity rather than a labeling of rungs, this reads as a well-instrumented replication with an aspirational law attached.

judges.strongest: This is the first design that randomizes the editable surface at a fixed optimizer with matched tokens, and it uses a blind-proposer control to separate space quality from proposer quality. The L4/L5 rungs (improver and archive editable) are a real gap that no prior ladder covers. Every outcome is publishable: an inverted U with a moving peak, a monotone curve, or a flat null all teach the field something about how openness differs between published systems. The timing is good. RobustSGPO, EvoSpace and HARNESSEVO have made the 'too closed vs too open' tension a live question without settling the interaction.
judges.weakest: 1. Openness is not one scalar. L0 to L5 change the representation (slots, then free text, then a typed DSL, then Python, then meta-code), not just the amount of freedom, so any 'peak at L2' may really be a 'typed DSL is a good inductive bias' effect. Fitting A(O) and B0(O) with O set to the rung index 0 to 5 is arbitrary. 2. The headline, the peak SHIFT, is badly underpowered. Bootstrapping the argmax over 6 noisy rungs with 5 seeds, then running a trend test over 3 capability tiers and 3 n_val levels, leaves very few independent points. On noisy tau2 or AppWorld the argmax CI will likely cover 3 or more rungs. 3. The 'law' has more free parameters than the cells can identify (A, B0 per rung, c, with N_eff measured), and its noise term is the existing PAC bounds. Reviewers will call it curve-fitting. 4. The compute is heavy for one undergrad. Roughly 270 or more lineages at 2M tokens, plus random-proposer and TTS arms, plus the n_val cross, comes to about 0.6 to 1B tokens with agentic executors, and L4/L5 sandboxing is serious engineering. 5. The 4B proposer will probably fail to produce valid L3 to L5 edits at all. That turns the capability axis into a trivial 'can't use the surface' effect rather than an optimum shift.
judges.mustFix: (a) Replace rung index with a measured, continuous openness coordinate per lineage. Candidates are the log-size or entropy of the realized edit distribution, or the number of distinct accepted behaviors (N_eff), and the design should report nominal vs realized vs effective space. Add at least one 'same openness, different representation' pair (e.g., an L2 DSL vs L3 restricted to the same operators) to separate representation from openness. (b) Run a power analysis now from the pilot seed SD. Shrink the grid to fit (e.g., 4 rungs: L1, L2, L3, L4/L5 merged; 2 tiers, 27B plus a frontier-mini; 8 to 10 seeds on the exact-evaluator task), and make CO-Bench the primary test, with tau2 confirmatory. (c) Pre-register the interaction as a direct contrast: does the gain difference between the adjacent rungs near the peak flip sign across tier or n_val? Do not use argmax-bootstrap as the main test. (d) Treat the law as an empirical test of the PAC/admission bounds (2609.08175, 2610.18813), with at most 3 free parameters, and validate it on held-out cells. Add a scheduled-openness arm as an out-of-sample prediction target. (e) Swap the 4B for a model tier that can produce valid edits at L3 and above (e.g., 14B), or report the validity rate per rung so that capability is not confounded with syntax failure. (f) Lead with the peak-shift interaction and cite RobustSGPO and EvoSpace as single-slice priors.
judges.reviewerQuote: The randomized-surface design is the right experiment, and the blind-proposer control is welcome. But the 'openness' axis mixes representation with freedom, and with 5 seeds the claimed peak shift falls within the bootstrap CI of the argmax. RobustSGPO already shows that an intermediate surface beats the most open one, so the remaining contribution is the interaction, and that is not established at this power. Borderline. I would raise my score if the interaction contrast were significant on the exact-evaluator task with a continuous, measured openness metric.

judges.strongest: Openness is the randomized treatment, with the optimizer and tokens held fixed. That is the right causal design for a debate that has so far run on confounded system-vs-system comparisons. The L4/L5 rungs, where the improver and the archive become editable, plus the random-proposer control, tie straight into the mentor's Gödel Agent line. They also turn the question "why don't meta-harnesses edit themselves?" into something you can measure: realized edits vs permitted edits per rung. Every outcome is publishable: inverted U, monotone, or flat.
judges.weakest: The headline peak-shift claim is underpowered and only weakly identifiable. You would be bootstrapping an argmax over 6 rungs with 5 noisy seeds per cell, then running a trend test on that argmax across 3 capability tiers. Expect confidence intervals spanning 2-3 rungs, which makes a 'shift' unprovable. Three more problems. The rungs are not one ordinal axis: the L2 typed DSL is not nested inside L3 Python, and L4/L5 change what is optimized, not just how much. A 4B proposer will almost never make valid L3-L5 edits, so its upper rungs collapse to nominal ones. The grid is also too large for a solo 6-month project: 6 rungs × 3 tiers × 3 tasks × 5 seeds × 2M tokens, plus the n_val cross and the random-proposer controls, plus tau2's user-simulator cost. Finally, "optimizer capability" is confounded with executor capability unless the executor is frozen.
judges.mustFix:
1. Freeze the executor model across all optimizer tiers, so that only proposer capability varies. Count proposer tokens and executor tokens separately.
2. Run a power analysis from the pilot seed SD before committing to the peak-shift headline. If the argmax CI exceeds 1 rung, change the pre-registered test to a parametric interaction (rung × tier slope in the hierarchical model) instead of an argmax trend.
3. Shrink the grid. Use 4 rungs (L1, L3, L4, L5; drop L0 and L2, or make L2 a side arm). Use 2 local tiers: replace the 4B with an ~8-9B model, and put the frontier-mini on 2 rungs only. Use 1 exact task plus 1 agentic task, with far-transfer as an evaluation of existing lineages, not a new grid. Cross n_val only at 2 levels.
4. Define openness by a measured quantity as well as the rung label: realized edit entropy or N_eff per rung. Fit the law on that measured quantity, so it holds up even if the rung ordering is contested.
5. Lead with the RobustSGPO/EvoSpace delta and frame the law as an empirical test of the existing PAC bounds, as the scoop check recommends.

The 'inverted U' itself was already shown in RobustSGPO. The fitted law adds a measured N_eff to known admission bounds without new theory. title: Gate, Not Willingness: A Causal Factorial of Why Self-Referential Improvers Rarely Edit Themselves
claim: In a self-referential harness loop with the improver code editable, the acceptance gate (an object-level one-step gate vs a separate meta gate with delayed credit) explains more variance in the retained improver-edit rate than permission framing and model family combined. Explicit framing raises the rate of proposed improver edits at least 5x but leaves the retained rate below 5% under the object-level gate.
alt: If framing or model family dominates (for example, retained meta-edits jump under explicit permission even with the object-level gate, or Qwen and Llama differ more than gate arms do), the low rate is a disposition, plausibly from post-training, and not a credit-assignment artifact. That would be the first causal measurement of the widely voiced self-modification-aversion hypothesis and would point to prompt or fine-tuning fixes rather than gate redesign, so it is publishable either way.
design: Shared testbed: GodelLite, a ~600-line loop whose editable surface is configurable over {prompt/memory, harness code, improver code (proposal policy plus selection and reflection logic)}. The outer evaluation and sandbox stay frozen. Tasks: 3 cheap auto-graded families (a LiveCodeBench-lite slice, a MATH-hard slice, a BFCL-style tool-calling slice). Each family has search, validation and held-out splits, and one whole family is held out per run for transfer. Factorial: framing {neutral repo-level instruction, explicit 'you may and should improve improver.py'} x gate {object-level single-step gate on validation score, separate meta gate scoring an improver edit by nested-replay successor quality k=3 generations later on frozen common states} x verification {off, on (improver edits must pass an improver-API test suite)} x model {Qwen3-32B, gpt-oss-120b, Llama-4-Scout, GLM-4.6}. That is 32 cells x 5 seeds = 160 runs of 20 generations. All arms get the same LLM-call and evaluation budget; the meta gate's replay cost is deducted from its generation budget. Outcomes: proposed and retained improver-edit rates, edits coded by an LLM annotator plus a structural diff classifier (agreement checked on 200 hand labels), and successor quality via nested replay (Improvement-by-Inheritance style), with held-out task score as secondary. Stats: mixed-effects logistic model for retention with seed as a random effect, eta-squared decomposition per factor, and preregistered contrasts. Cost: about $1.2k at hosted open-model prices.
law: Retention logit model: logit P(retain meta) = b0 + b_gate*G + b_frame*F + b_ver*V + b_model + interactions. Prediction: |b_gate| > |b_frame| + range(b_model), and the F x G interaction is positive (framing helps only when the gate can see meta value).
pilot: Qwen3-32B only, code family only, 2x2 (framing x gate), 3 seeds x 10 generations, about $45. Go if the object-gate arm reproduces a natural retained improver-edit rate below 5% and explicit framing raises proposals at least 3x. Kill or reframe if retained meta-edits already exceed 20% under the object gate with neutral framing, which would mean the phenomenon does not reproduce on open models.

title: Why Improvers Don't Improve Themselves: A Factorial on the Self-Edit Drought and a Drift Benchmark That Makes Self-Editing Necessary
claim: Neither permission nor prompt framing produces self-edits that help. The meta-edit rate and successor quality are driven by improver-level evidence: a counterfactual ledger showing which of the improver's own past edit types paid off on held-out. Under a drift stream where the improver's dominant edit type stops paying, improvers fed this evidence lose at most half as much held-out score after each shift as fixed or permission-only improvers, at matched compute.
alt: If permission or salience alone recovers the benefit, then the drought is a framing artifact (consistent with SelfImprove-Bench's 0→45%). The practical fix becomes 'just prompt it', which is cheap, decisive and publishable. If no condition helps under drift, then self-editing is not the bottleneck for continual adaptation, which argues against the RSI agenda with clean evidence.
design: MetaLite at L4: the improver's prompt and its selection/analysis code are editable. 2×2×2×2 factorial: permission (improver editable or not) × salience (improver self-edit named explicitly in the charter or not) × improver-level evidence (an auto-generated ledger of past edit types with same-start held-out swap deltas, computed by the harness) × credit horizon (whether a self-edit is credited by its children's one-step gain or by k=3-step successor gain via nested replay, as in Inheritance). 16 cells × 5 lineages. Stream: VersionShift-Drift, 4 phases. Phase 1 failures are prompt-addressable (missing instructions). Phase 2 failures need a tool or helper (a real API rename). Phase 3 needs control flow (retries and version detection). Phase 4 needs a gate or selection change (noisy validation, where the improver must adopt paired testing). Each phase uses real library-changelog items in pinned containers, with held-out task sets per phase. Compute is matched by rollouts and by proposer tokens, and self-edits cost the same budget as object edits. Models: local Qwen3-8B as task agent, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B as improver, with a DeepSeek replication for 2 cells. Primary metrics: meta-edit rate, successor quality (the held-out gain of children produced by the edited improver vs the unedited one from the same start), and post-shift drop and recovery time per phase. Stats: ANOVA or a mixed model over factors, paired bootstrap on drop. Mechanism analysis: code each self-edit (selection, analysis prompt, budget allocation) and test whether the evidence ledger causes the right type of edit for the phase.
law: n/a. Secondary hypothesis: meta-edit rate ∝ salience × P(improver-level evidence available), and successor quality ∝ evidence × horizon, with a significant interaction and no main effect of permission.
pilot: Week 1: 4 cells (permission only; permission+salience; permission+evidence; fixed improver) × 2 lineages, on phases 1→2 only (about 80 tasks). Under $40 API. Go if the evidence cell's meta-edit rate is at least 2× the permission-only cell, and its phase-2 drop is smaller than the fixed improver's by more than seed SD. Kill if all 4 cells show a meta-edit rate under 5% (pivot to measuring the drought as the result) or the phase shift causes no measurable drop (rebuild the drift stream).
closest: Improvement by Inheritance (ZMmJDeDTXk): shows the drought and an evidence-fed modifier, but uses replay on fixed Hyperagents history with no factorial and no drift. SelfImprove-Bench HyperDSH (2611.02797): manipulates framing only. Predict Before You Modify (ZBxV5bEYUH) and HMED (2610.07979): give the improver evidence, but not as a factorial against permission and salience. MetaRSI (2609.06396) and RSI-Harness (EOrtreQLbv): optimize the optimizer on stationary tasks. AgentStream and continual-learning benchmarks test the task agent, not the improver. What is new here: a causal decomposition of the drought plus a benchmark grounded in real library drift, in which each phase shift deliberately invalidates the improver's current edit habit, which forces continual meta-learning.

I found nothing that runs the causal decomposition (permission × salience × improver-level evidence × credit horizon) on the meta-edit rate. I also found no drift stream built so that each phase invalidates the improver's current edit habit. Both remain new. However, the 'evidence drives successor quality' half is largely pre-empted: Improvement by Inheritance's evidence-fed modifier already gives a successor-quality gain, and SelfLineage already tests descendant-aware evidence. Flex-RSI already forces a 4-round review of which edit types paid off.

To survive:
(1) Lead with the drift benchmark and the 'habit invalidation' result, not with 'evidence helps'. The headline should be that under VersionShift-Drift, improvers' edit-type distribution stays locked on the phase-1 habit (prompt or memory edits) after shifts. Then show which manipulation unlocks it and by how much recovery time shrinks. Pre-register the evidence main effect as a replication of ZMmJDeDTXk. judges.strongest: The causal decomposition of the self-edit drought (permission x salience x evidence) is something no prior paper runs as an intervention. Prior work is either observational (Opinionated Optimizers) or varies one lever (SelfImprove-Bench, framing only). The drift stream is built so that each phase makes the improver's current edit habit stop paying, so phase 4 (noisy validation, where only a gate or selection edit helps) can show whether self-editing becomes necessary. Every outcome is publishable: interaction only, framing artifact, or no help under drift.
judges.weakest: Three problems. (1) Novelty is half pre-empted: Inheritance (ZMmJDeDTXk) already shows that an evidence-fed improver gets better successors, and SelfLineage and Flex-RSI already cover descendant-aware ledgers and edit-type review, so the predicted big main effect is not new. (2) The ledger carries held-out swap deltas that are computed by the harness and not charged to the improver. That leaks held-out data into the improver's decisions and gives the evidence arm free compute, which breaks both the held-out claim and the matched-compute claim. (3) The phases always run in the order prompt, tool, control, gate, so phase type is confounded with lineage age and accumulated edits. With 16x5 lineages over 4 phases on a 30B improver, interaction tests are underpowered, and the engineering is too much for one undergrad. There is also a floor-effect risk: a 30B-A3B improver may be unable to write useful selection-code edits, in which case the drought is just a capability limit.

title: How Much Should an Improver Be Forced to Rewrite Itself? An Inverted-U Dose-Response for Mandated Meta-Edits at Matched Compute
claim: Forcing a fraction q of generations to edit the improver yields an inverted-U in successor quality. Without execution verification every q>0 is no better than the natural rate (q=0). With verification the optimum q* lies between 0.1 and 0.25 and shrinks as gate noise grows.
alt: If successor quality rises monotonically in q, the conservative natural rate is a pure bottleneck and systems should be maximally self-referential. If it is flat everywhere, forced meta-edits carry nothing beyond inheritance, which would confirm the Improvement by Inheritance and Learning-to-Repair results at scale. Each outcome settles the 'bug or feature' debate (Debate 1) with a dose-response rather than a single on/off ablation.
design: GodelLite with all three surfaces editable. Arms: quota q in {0 (natural), 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0}, where at a forced generation the proposer must emit an improver.py diff (non-empty AST change) and other generations are unconstrained. Crossed with verification {off, on} and gate noise {low: 200 validation items, high: 40 validation items}. That is 20 cells x 5 seeds = 100 runs. Model: Qwen3-32B as improver and task agent, with gpt-oss-120b as a replication at the 3 key q values. Budget is matched per run in LLM tokens and task evaluations; forced and unforced generations cost the same. Primary metric: nested-replay successor quality of the final improver, applied to 3 frozen common harness states for 4 generations on held-out tasks. Secondary metrics: held-out task score, meta-edit revert rate, and rerun reproducibility of acceptance decisions (VERSE-style). Fit a quadratic and a two-segment model of q, with bootstrap CIs on q*. Test the predicted negative interaction q* x noise with a preregistered contrast. Cost: about $900.
law: Successor gain G(q) ~ a*q - b*q^2*(sigma_gate/delta)^2 with verification lowering b. This gives q* = a / (2b (sigma/delta)^2), so the optimal forcing rate falls with the square of the gate's noise-to-effect ratio.
pilot: Verification on, low noise, q in {0, 0.25, 1.0}, 3 seeds x 12 generations on the code family, about $50. Go if q=0.25 beats both q=0 and q=1.0 on successor quality by at least 1 SE in 2 of 3 seeds, or if q=1.0 is clearly worse than q=0.25 (curvature exists). Kill if all three arms fall within noise; in that case pivot to the code-vs-state transplant as the main result.
closest: VERSE 2610.02616 (binary self-evolution on/off, 1 run per cell); MetaRSI 2609.06396 and Flex-RSI 2611.08946 (mandated meta-steps, never ablating the mandate rate); MetaSkill-Evolve 2607.05297 (H sweep confounded with iteration count, no seeds); Improvement by Inheritance ZMmJDeDTXk (successor-quality assay, which we reuse). Delta: the first matched-compute dose-response on the forcing rate itself, crossed with verification and gate noise, scored by successor quality rather than task score.

Sec 4.4 and App. Table 2 sweep H in {2,4,8} with the number of meta-updates fixed at 3, so total iterations = 3H. H=2 is best on all three benchmarks (OfficeQA 48.9 to 39.8). check.reposition:
No paper I found sweeps a forced improver-edit quota q at matched compute, crosses it with verification and gate noise, and scores it by successor quality. The specific design is open. Its parts are not. VERSE already owns 'verification is necessary for meta-edits'. The Winner's Curse (2610.09239) already owns the selection-under-noise theory and the validation-size noise manipulation. MetaSkill-Evolve already ran a (confounded, single-seed) meta-cadence sweep and found monotone 'more frequent is better'. Reviewers are likely to call this a hyperparameter sweep with a textbook law. To survive:

(1) Make the law predictive, not post hoc. Estimate the proposal mean and spread of improver edits (mu_meta, s_meta) and the gate noise sigma from a cheap oracle pilot, as the Winner's Curse paper does. Pre-register a predicted q* for each noise cell before running the grid. The claim becomes 'the winner's-curse model with a compounding term predicts where forcing stops helping'. Add the compounding term explicitly: a harmful improver edit degrades every later proposal, unlike a harmful prompt edit. That gives a b-term scaling with the remaining horizon, which neither Winner's Curse nor VERSE has.

(2) Separate forcing as exploration from forcing as content. Add a placebo arm in which forced generations must make a semantically null AST change (rename or reorder). Add a forced-then-reverted-unless-verified arm. A 'non-empty AST diff' is trivially gameable by Qwen3-32B, so report the edit-semantics distribution for each q.

(3) Include EvoLyapunov-style adaptive gating and MetaSkill-Evolve-style fixed cadence (every k = 1/q generations, deterministic rather than random) as baselines. That shows whether random quota, cadence or adaptive triggering matters, and answers 'why not just use an adaptive gate'.

(4) Fix the matched-compute confound MetaSkill-Evolve had: same generations and evaluations for every q, which the design already does, so state it as the contrast with MetaSkill-Evolve.

(5) Report the VERSE-style rerun reproducibility of meta-edit accept decisions as the measured sigma, so the noise axis is measured, not only manipulated.

(6) Hedge the headline. If the result is monotone (MetaSkill-Evolve's prior) or flat (VERSE's Terminal-Bench result), the paper still stands as 'a measured dose-response plus a falsified or confirmed noise law'. Pre-register both outcomes.

It answers with a dose-response at matched compute, scored by successor quality (the ZMmJDeDTXk assay) rather than by task score. The design crosses forcing rate with verification and gate noise, which turns 'verification matters' (VERSE) and 'noise matters' (Winner's Curse) into one testable interaction. The q-by-noise contrast is preregistered. Monotone, flat and inverted-U results are each interpretable. Qwen3-32B plus gpt-oss-120b keeps it open-weights and affordable. Winner's Curse owns the noise-to-effect selection theory, and it already manipulates validation-set size, so the 200 vs 40 noise arms are its manipulation. MetaSkill-Evolve already swept meta-cadence and found 'more frequent is better'. Run a simulation-based power analysis on pilot variance to pick seeds, probably 8-10 in the key cells. (3) Match total evaluation cost across noise arms, or manipulate noise by injecting label noise or a stochastic grader at a fixed item count. Report the measured rerun-reproducibility sigma, VERSE-style. (4) Add a placebo arm that forces a semantically null edit, and a forced-but-reverted-unless-verified arm. Report the edit-semantics distribution per q. (5) Add fixed-cadence (every 1/q generations, MetaSkill-Evolve) and an EvoLyapunov-style adaptive gate as baselines. (6) Cite and differentiate VERSE, Winner's Curse, MetaSkill-Evolve, Flex-RSI, SelfImprove-Bench, IFR, MetaRSI, RSI-Harness, EvoLyapunov, Masked Erosion and Recoverability & Verifier Strength. (7) Budget realistically. With the nested replay (3 states x 4 generations of held-out evaluation per final improver), $9/run is optimistic. Plan for $1.5-2.5k and keep a fallback reduced grid.
judges.reviewerQuote: The question matters and the successor-quality metric is the right one, but as written this is a hyperparameter sweep stapled to the winner's-curse inequality. The grid is too coarse and the seeds too few to localize the claimed q*, and the validation-size noise arm is both borrowed from 2610.09239 and compute-confounded. I would move to accept only if the authors preregister a quantitative q* from pilot-estimated parameters, include a horizon-compounding term that prior theory lacks, and show the prediction holds, with a placebo-edit arm ruling out the possibility that forcing helps merely by injecting exploration.

judges.strongest: The axis being studied is real and nobody has measured it. Every paper uses a fixed meta-cadence (MetaRSI, Flex-RSI, RSI-Harness, IFR) or a binary on/off switch (VERSE), and the only sweep (MetaSkill-Evolve) is confounded with iteration count. A matched-compute dose-response, scored by successor quality and crossed with verification and gate noise, would be a clean descriptive contribution. It also bears directly on the debate over why meta-harnesses rarely edit themselves. Every outcome (inverted-U, monotone, flat) has a pre-registered reading.
judges.weakest:
On its own this is a hyperparameter sweep plus a textbook law. The law G(q) ~ a*q - b*q^2*(sigma/delta)^2 is the Winner's Curse (2610.09239) applied to meta-edits. VERSE already owns 'verification is needed'. Winner's Curse already owns the 200-vs-40 validation-size noise manipulation. So the factorial is VERSE x Winner's Curse x a q axis, which is close to K4.

The quadratic form is also ad hoc. Nothing in the setup derives the q^2 term: harmful edits that compound would give a horizon-dependent term, not q^2.

Three practical problems:
- A 'non-empty AST diff' mandate is trivially gamed by Qwen3-32B, so high-q arms may measure no-op churn.
- With 5 seeds and 5 q levels on noisy successor-quality estimates, the bootstrap CI on q* will likely cover the whole 0.1 to 0.5 range. That would make the q* x noise interaction contrast underpowered.
- About $900 for 100 runs, each with nested replay (3 states x 4 generations on held-out tasks) plus a gpt-oss-120b replication, looks optimistic by 2-3x.
judges.mustFix:
Make the law predictive and derive it properly:
- Measure proposal mean and spread for improver edits (mu_meta, s_meta) and the gate noise sigma in an oracle pilot.
- Derive a compounding term in which a harmful improver edit taxes every remaining generation, so b scales with the horizon H. The horizon dependence is something neither Winner's Curse nor VERSE has.
- Pre-register a numeric q* for each noise cell before running the grid.

Add a placebo arm that forces semantically null AST edits, plus an edit-semantics audit for each q, to separate exploration from content.

Add the obvious baselines:
- deterministic cadence k = 1/q, MetaSkill-Evolve style
- an EvoLyapunov adaptive gate

Cut the grid to fund power. Drop q=1.0 or use only 3 noise/verification cells, and raise the seed count to 8 or more at the q values that bracket q*. Run a power analysis on the pilot variance before committing.

Re-check the ICLR 2027 revisions of VERSE and IFR for frequency ablations.
judges.reviewerQuote: "This is a careful sweep of one hyperparameter, and the proposed 'law' is the winner's-curse selection model with q substituted in. I'd raise my score if the authors predicted q* ahead of time from pilot-estimated noise, and showed that the optimum moves with horizon length because harmful improver edits compound. Without that, it reads as a well-run ablation that VERSE's appendix could have contained."

judges.strongest: This turns the "is the improver's reluctance to rewrite itself a bug or a feature" debate into a matched-compute dose-response, scored by successor quality instead of task score. That fits the mentor's Gödel Agent line closely. Nobody has swept the forcing rate q with seeds and crossed it with verification and gate noise. MetaSkill-Evolve's sweep is confounded with iteration count and has no seeds. VERSE, MetaRSI and Flex-RSI only test on/off or fixed cadences. A cheap $50 pilot gives a clean go/kill signal on curvature, and there is a fallback (the code-vs-state transplant).
judges.weakest:
Every piece is owned by someone else, so a reviewer will likely read it as a hyperparameter sweep. VERSE owns the claim that unverified meta-edits don't help. Winner's Curse (2610.09239) owns the noise-to-effect law and the 200-vs-40 validation-size noise manipulation. The proposed G(q) = a*q - b*q^2*(sigma/delta)^2 is that law relabelled. The predicted range q* in [0.1, 0.25] is picked by hand, not derived.

The statistics are also weak. The nested-replay successor-quality metric is noisy, and 5 seeds per cell across 5 q levels is probably too few to put a bootstrap CI on a quadratic peak or to detect the q* x noise interaction. The likely result is "flat within noise", which is the K2-adjacent outcome. The rule that a forced generation must produce a "non-empty AST diff" is easy for Qwen3-32B to game with cosmetic edits. Without a placebo arm, forcing-as-exploration can't be separated from forcing-as-content.

On cost: 100 runs plus a gpt-oss replication plus the reviewer-requested placebo and adaptive-gate baselines will push past the $900 estimate. The space is also very crowded, with roughly ten 2026 papers on adjacent points.
judges.mustFix:
1. Make the law predictive and genuinely new. Estimate mu_meta, s_meta and sigma_gate from an oracle pilot. Derive a compounding-horizon term: a harmful improver edit damages every later proposal, so b should scale with the remaining generations. Then pre-register numeric q* predictions for each noise cell before running the grid. Without this step the paper is Winner's Curse applied to meta-edits.

2. Add a placebo arm in which forced edits must be semantically null, plus a forced-but-reverted-unless-verified arm. Report the distribution of edit semantics at each q.

3. Run a power analysis on pilot variance. Then reshape the grid: drop the verification-off half to a single q=0 vs q=0.25 contrast (VERSE already covers it), and spend the freed budget on more seeds and a third noise level, so the interaction becomes a slope rather than a two-point contrast.

4. Add the EvoLyapunov adaptive gate and a deterministic cadence (every 1/q generations) as baselines.

5. Pre-register the monotone and flat outcomes so a null result still publishes as a falsified law.
judges.reviewerQuote: "The authors run a carefully controlled sweep of a single hyperparameter and fit a quadratic whose form follows directly from the winner's-curse analysis of 2610.09239. The verification-off half reproduces VERSE. With 5 seeds and a noisy successor-quality assay, the claimed inverted-U is not distinguishable from flat in Fig. 3, and the q* x noise interaction rests on two noise levels. I would be more positive if the compounding term had been derived and its predicted q* pre-registered and confirmed out of sample."

title: When the Grader Moves: Real Verifier-Commit Drift Is What Makes Self-Improvers Rewrite Their Acceptance Gate
claim: Replaying real verifier and benchmark-harness commits (BenchPulse-mined) under a frozen task pool raises the rate at which a Gödel-lite agent edits its own acceptance gate or improver from about 0% to at least 15% of retained edits. A gate-editable arm then keeps at least 50% fewer stale accepted edits than a frozen-gate arm, measured on held-out tasks graded by the post-commit verifier.
alt: If gate-edit rates stay near 0 and stale-edit retention matches the frozen arm even when the feedback channel changes, then no ordinary environmental pressure induces meta-level change. That strongly supports building improver-forcing mechanisms (scheduled revalidation, explicit meta-budgets) into harness designs, and it is publishable as the clean negative that resolves the 'bug or artefact' debate the review flags.
law: Retained stale edits decay as exp(−t/τ) after a verifier commit. The prediction is that τ is at least 2× shorter in the gate-editable arm, and that τ scales with commit score impact |Δ| (larger |Δ| gives a shorter τ only when S5 is editable).
pilot:
Use 1 benchmark (τ-bench retail, a subset of 60 tasks), 2 real verifier states around the −5.66 pp commit, arms (a) and (c), 3 lineages, a local Qwen3-32B, and about $30 of API calls.
Go if both hold: at least 10% of accepted V0 edits flip benefit under V1, which shows the commit actually stresses retained edits; and arm (c) makes at least one gate edit in at least 2 of 3 lineages.
Kill if fewer than 5% of edits flip. That would mean real verifier drift is too gentle, and the stream should switch to a larger-impact BFCL aggregation change.
closest: BenchPulse hpoWWEDJW9 provides the census of real verifier drift but no learning agent; the delta is using it as a stream for a self-improver. Breaking-the-improver and gate-dial (prior rounds) use fixed judges and static gates. AgentDriftBench 5xFWggnePr provides recovery metrics but injects environment drift and includes no improver. Are-SE-CL 2610.25858 observes that the Meta-Harness gate freezes but never perturbs the gate's feedback source. SelfImprove-Bench 2611.02797 sees 0% improver edits on stationary graders.

closestFound.title: When the Evaluator Changes: Measuring False Progress in Self-Improving Language Models (ICLR 2027 submission)
closestFound.summary: Studies 'false progress' when the evaluator is revised during self-improvement. Uses a cross-version evaluation matrix (each model version scored under each evaluator version), a progress decomposition, and Loom, a replayable dataflow that tracks which supervision fed which update and whether the model state can recover after the evaluator is repaired. Experiments are controlled RL post-training.
closestFound.overlap: High on measurement. It already covers the evaluator-revision framing, the stale-progress idea, and recoverability after an evaluator fix, and it is the most likely reviewer comparison for the stale-accepted-edits and verifier-overfit-gap metrics. It differs in that it does weight-level RL rather than a harness self-improver, uses synthetic or controlled evaluator revisions rather than mined real verifier commits, and has no editable acceptance gate and no measure of how often gate or improver edits happen.

closestFound.title: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators
closestFound.summary: Recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities, where learned evaluators (a reviewer agent, graders) co-evolve with the coder or prover. Reports gains over a fixed-evaluator baseline on DeepSWE, paper writing and IMO grading.
closestFound.overlap: Medium. It claims the 'non-stationary evaluator in a Gödel-style loop' framing. But the evaluator change is endogenous and designed in. It does not replay real exogenous grader commits, does not measure whether the agent itself edits its gate, and does not measure stale edits. Its forward citations (VeriEvolve 2610.29005, Verifier-Harness Co-Evolution 2610.17609, Evo² 2610.13025, Self-Modifying Lean Proof Agents 2607.17352) are all co-evolution designs, none drift replay.

closestFound.title: Gödel Ecology: Productivity-Guided Continuous Co-Evolution of Agents and Evaluators
closestFound.summary: Continuous co-evolution of self-improving coding agents and a soft mixture of evaluators. Includes delayed credit assignment and adversarial interventions against self-reinforcing evaluator drift.
closestFound.overlap: Medium. It contains 'evaluator drift' and evaluator updates inside Gödel-style RSI, but the drift is generated by the system itself. There is no real verifier-commit stream and no comparison of gate-editable versus frozen-gate arms.

closestFound.title: BenchPulse: Monitoring Verdict and Ranking Drift in Evolving Agent Benchmarks
closestFound.summary: Census of 4,119 commits across 15 agent benchmarks. A single τ-bench verifier commit moves scores by -5.66 pp, a τ²-bench release moves model panels by up to 9 pp, and a BFCL aggregation change reverses 893 pairwise orderings. Includes a replay panel for re-evaluation.
closestFound.overlap: Data source only. It covers exactly the commits the idea plans to mine, with no learning agent. If BenchPulse publishes its commit list, the data-mining contribution shrinks, so the novelty has to come from the self-improver behavior.

closestFound.title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents
closestFound.summary: 411 improvement loops under ten acceptance-gate rules, plus GEPA. Shows that the gate fails to see redundant safeguards being deleted, and fits a pre-registered statistical model of where each gate breaks.
closestFound.overlap: Low to medium. It treats the acceptance gate as the object of study and builds a predictive law, but the gate rules are fixed by the experimenter, the grader does not move, and the agent never edits its own gate.

closestFound.title: Feedback Alignment in Self-Improving Agents

closestFound.overlap: Medium on the 'verifier-overfit gap' metric (intended grader versus current verifier). The V/T split is static, with no drift over time and no editing of the gate.
