check.reposition: I found no paper that replays real, mined verifier or benchmark-harness commits as a stream for a self-improver, or that tests whether grader drift is what causes gate or improver self-edits. The behavioral core of the idea is open. The framing nearby is crowded, though: evaluator revision and false progress (tn4eslVXEK), co-evolving evaluators (Red Queen Gödel Machine, Gödel Ecology, 2610.11464), and the visible-versus-target overfit gap (C6EElQ2PRG). Changes to survive review: (1) Lead with the causal behavioral claim: exogenous, real grader maintenance moves the gate/improver edit share from about 0% to at least 15%, and the shuffled-commit-order control and a synthetic-drift control with matched |Δ| should show that real commits differ from injected noise. Put the stale-edit and overfit-gap metrics second. (2) Present the metrics as an extension of tn4eslVXEK's cross-version matrix to harness-level self-improvement with an editable gate, and say explicitly that the evaluator change here is exogenous. Co-evolution papers control their own evaluator, and real benchmarks change underneath you. (3) Add an arm where the agent sees the verifier diff or changelog versus one where it only sees feedback, to separate 'notices drift' from 'can act on drift'. (4) Treat the exp(−t/τ) law as a secondary, pre-registered prediction, following Masked Erosion's frozen-model style, not as the headline. Most real commits are bug fixes, so the |Δ| range may be narrow. Get BenchPulse's commit list early, and pick commits that cover a wide range of |Δ|, including sign flips. (5) Include an arm that edits the gate under a stationary grader, to rule out 'S5 is simply exposed more' as the explanation.

judges.strongest: The question is causal and directly answers the user's 'why doesn't the meta-harness update itself' debate. It uses exogenous, real grader maintenance as a natural experiment, which no co-evolution paper does: in those papers the system controls its own evaluator, and SelfImprove-Bench and Are-SE-CL only observe the 0% baseline. Both outcomes are informative, a reusable replay harness made of pinned verifier checkouts can come out of it, and relevance to self-referential meta-agents is high.
judges.weakest: The mechanism and the power are both thin. The agent sees only score feedback, so a verifier commit looks like an unexplained regression, and nothing in the design says why the right fix is a gate edit rather than an object-level patch. Gate editing also does not mechanically remove stale edits; only revalidation does. Arm (c) could 'win' by loosening its gate or reward-hacking the new verifier, and stale-edit counts alone would not tell those apart from real adaptation. There are only about 9 real commit transitions in total (3 benchmarks x 3 steps). Most are narrow bug fixes, and a -5.66 pp commit on a 60-task subset touches roughly 3 to 4 tasks, so the 10% flip go-criterion is likely to fail. Fitting a tau-vs-|Delta| law on about 9 points with 5 lineages each is not credible. On scooping, tn4eslVXEK already owns the stale-progress and verifier-overfit metrics, so the novelty rests entirely on the behavioral gate-edit claim.
judges.mustFix: (1) Add a synthetic-drift control matched on |Delta| and on which tasks are affected, plus a stationary-grader arm with the gate editable, so that 'real drift causes meta edits' is identifiable and not just 'S5 is exposed' or 'any score drop'. (2) Add a diff/changelog-visible arm against a feedback-only arm. (3) Classify every gate edit by type (tightening, loosening, revalidation trigger) and report gate edits that hack the post-commit verifier, scored by the intended grader. Without that, a higher gate-edit rate is uninterpretable. (4) Get the BenchPulse commit list in week 1 and choose commits that span a wide |Delta| range, including sign flips. If fewer than about 6 usable transitions exist, drop the tau law to an exploratory appendix. (5) Budget the tau-bench user-simulator LLM calls and GPU rental for 5 arms x 5 lineages x 3 benchmarks x 4 states. This probably means cutting to 2 benchmarks and 3 core arms (a, c, plus synthetic) to stay within $3k, with a second open model (for example Llama or GLM) rather than only an API check. (6) Run a blind audit of a sample of edit attributions, because the S4/S5 classification drives the headline number.
judges.reviewerQuote: The use of real verifier commits as an exogenous shock is a clever natural experiment. But with roughly nine transitions, mostly small bug fixes, and no control for any score regression of matched size, I cannot tell whether the agent is responding to grader drift or simply to regressions. I also cannot tell whether a gate edit means adaptation or that the agent learned to lower its own bar. The metrics largely restate tn4eslVXEK at the harness level.

judges.strongest: The causal question is concrete, falsifiable, and new: does exogenous, real grader maintenance push an agent to edit its own gate or improver? It speaks directly to the user's question about why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves. It is also grounded in reality, because it uses mined commits instead of synthetic drift, and that is a real point of difference from the co-evolution papers (Red Queen GM, Gödel Ecology), where the system controls its own evaluator. Arm (d), the oracle revalidation procedure, together with the shuffled-order control, gives a clean ceiling and a clean null reference.
judges.weakest: The signal is likely too thin, and the main effect has confounds. (1) Most real verifier commits are small bug fixes. On 60 tasks, a -5.66 pp commit changes about 3 or 4 task verdicts, so "edits whose benefit flips sign" will be a handful of events per lineage. With 3 to 5 lineages, the negative-binomial GLM and the fitted exp(-t/τ) will be badly underpowered, and the τ-vs-|Δ| law rests on perhaps 3 to 4 commit points per benchmark with a narrow |Δ| range. (2) The gate-edit share is confounded by exposure and by reward hacking. An editable S5 under a moving grader can "reduce stale edits" just by loosening or resetting the gate, which inflates held-out-under-current-verifier scores without tracking the intended grader. You need a gate-edit-under-stationary-grader arm and a classification of gate edits (tighten, revalidate, loosen). (3) Qwen3-32B may never edit S5 in either condition. Then you get a 0% versus 0% null, which is a weak paper next to SelfImprove-Bench's existing 0% finding. (4) Scope is large for a solo undergrad: 3 benchmarks x 4 pinned verifier states x 5 arms x 5 lineages x 2 models, plus τ-bench user simulation, plus a human-validated intended grader. (5) Novelty hinges on tn4eslVXEK. Reviewers will read the paper as "tn4eslVXEK's evaluator-revision false-progress setup moved to a harness loop with BenchPulse data", which is borderline K4.
judges.mustFix: Make the headline the causal edit-rate claim and power it properly. Pick commits from BenchPulse's census that are high-|Δ| or flip signs, aiming for at least 15% task-verdict churn. Use at least 150 tasks per benchmark, or stack several commits. Run at least 8 lineages for the arms that matter, (a), (c), and a stationary-grader gate-editable arm (c0), and cut the other arms and benchmarks to one benchmark plus one replication. Add a synthetic-drift control with matched |Δ| and a changelog-visible versus feedback-only arm. Code every gate edit as tighten, revalidate, or loosen, and report the intended-grader score as the primary outcome so that gate loosening cannot count as a win. Pre-register the τ law as secondary. Cite tn4eslVXEK explicitly and frame your setup as its extension to harness-level, exogenous, real-commit drift.
judges.reviewerQuote: The question of whether real grader drift induces meta-level self-modification is interesting and under-explored. However, only a handful of tasks actually change verdict per commit, and the gate-editable arm can reduce 'stale edits' by simply relaxing its acceptance criteria. Without a stationary-grader gate-editable control and edit-type coding, I cannot distinguish adaptive revalidation from gate erosion. The proposed decay law is fit to too few commit events to be meaningful. Relative to 'When the Evaluator Changes' (tn4eslVXEK), the contribution reads as a port to a harness loop. Weak reject, would raise with a properly powered single-benchmark study.

judges.strongest: This tests the user's question directly: does real, outside pressure, not a designed curriculum, make a self-improver change its own meta-level? It does this with actual mined grader commits, which is concrete and hard to dismiss. As far as the scoop check found, no prior work treats exogenous verifier churn as the stream for a harness self-improver with an editable gate. That puts it squarely in Yin's Gödel Agent territory, and the cross-version framing gives a natural extension of tn4eslVXEK.
judges.weakest: The mechanism is underspecified, and the obvious outcome is a boring null. If every gate decision already re-scores candidates under the current verifier, a frozen gate is never 'stale'. Staleness only exists if earlier accepted edits are never re-checked, and then the oracle arm (d) is the whole answer while arm (c) depends on the LLM spontaneously writing revalidation logic. SelfImprove-Bench already reports 0% improver edits. So '~0% gate edits even under drift' is the likely result. It is publishable only as a minor confirmation, not as a resolution of the 'bug or artefact' debate. Real verifier commits are mostly small bug fixes: the |Δ| range is narrow and there are only about 4 events per benchmark. That makes the exp(-t/τ) law and the |Δ|-scaling claim close to impossible to estimate. Then there is scale: 5 arms × 5 lineages × 4 states × 3 benchmarks, with Qwen3-32B as both agent and τ-bench user simulator, on a modest GPU. That is well beyond what one undergrad can run in 6 months.
judges.mustFix: (1) Before the pilot, pin down the gate semantics. What exactly is in S5? Does the gate keep cached scores for retained edits? What can a gate edit actually change: revalidation, thresholds, or which verifier signals it reads? Show that a frozen gate really carries stale edits forward; otherwise the stale-edit metric is zero by construction. (2) Cut to 1–2 benchmarks and 3 arms: frozen gate, gate-editable, and a gate-editable arm under a stationary grader (this rules out the explanation that S5 is simply more exposed). Add one synthetic-drift control with matched |Δ|; drop shuffled-order and the multi-benchmark breadth. (3) Add the diff/changelog-visible arm. It is the cheapest way to get a positive result, and it separates 'notices drift' from 'can act on drift'. (4) Make the headline the causal edit-rate claim. Report τ only as a descriptive, pre-registered secondary result, and choose commits with sign flips so |Δ| varies. (5) Budget the τ-bench user simulator explicitly. Use a smaller local simulator or a cached API simulator, and check that $3k covers 2 models × lineages.
judges.reviewerQuote: The question is interesting: does real benchmark maintenance push self-improvers to edit their own acceptance criteria? But the paper never makes clear why a gate that already scores against the current verifier would hold stale edits in the first place, and the oracle revalidation arm suggests the fix is a two-line procedure, not emergent meta-learning. With four commits per benchmark, the decay law is effectively a fit through four points, and the near-zero gate-edit rate largely restates SelfImprove-Bench.

title: Sharing Starves the Meta-Level: Population-Genetic Modifier Theory Predicts That Cross-Lineage Edit Sharing Suppresses Improver Self-Edits
claim: In a multi-lineage self-improving population, raising the rate r at which accepted harness edits are shared across lineages monotonically lowers the retained improver-edit frequency and the final improver's successor quality. Attributing shared edits back to the improver that generated them (clade credit) restores both.
alt: If sharing has no effect on meta-edit retention, improver edits survive through their direct effects rather than by hitchhiking on the edits they produce. That rules out a linkage-based design worry for MetaShare- and Looped-RSI-style systems and shows the low natural rate is not a population-structure artifact. Combined with a calibrated null, this is still a clean, publishable negative from a cross-field prediction.
design: Lens: in evolutionary biology, mutation-rate and evolvability modifier alleles are selected only indirectly, by hitchhiking with the beneficial mutations they cause. Recombination breaks this linkage, and modifiers then drift or are purged when they carry any cost. Mapping: improver edits are modifiers, harness edits are their products, and cross-lineage sharing of harness edits acts as recombination. Testbed: GodelLite population of 8 lineages, each with its own editable improver and harness. Every generation, each accepted harness edit is copied into other lineages with probability r in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0}, and acceptance is gated per lineage on held-out-of-search validation. A 5th arm uses r=1.0 with clade credit: a lineage's improver-edit selection score includes the gains its shared edits produce elsewhere (CMP-style attribution). 5 arms x 5 seeds (populations) x 15 generations. Model: Qwen3-14B for both roles (cheap, self-hostable), with a Qwen3-32B replication at r in {0, 1}. Compute is matched per population. Metrics: retained improver-edit frequency trajectory, measured selection coefficient of improver edits (Price-equation decomposition of the change in improver-edit frequency into direct and indirect, product-linked components), nested-replay successor quality on held-out tasks, and population-best held-out score. Preregistered test: a Jonckheere-Terpstra trend in r and the clade-credit vs r=1 contrast. Cost: about $800.
law: Modifier dynamics: delta p ~ p(1-p) * [s_ind * h * (1 - r) - c], where s_ind is the improver edit's effect on the beneficial-edit rate, h is product heritability within the lineage, and c is the direct cost. This predicts a critical sharing rate r* = 1 - c/(s_ind h) above which improver edits are purged, and that clade credit restores the effective (1 - r) term to about 1.
pilot: r in {0, 1.0} plus clade-credit, 3 populations x 4 lineages x 8 generations, Qwen3-14B on the code family, about $40. Go if retained improver-edit frequency at r=0 is at least 2x that at r=1.0, or if the Price decomposition shows a non-zero indirect component at r=0. Kill if improver edits are essentially absent in all arms (base rate too low to measure); in that case run on top of the forced-quota arm (q=0.25) so that proposals exist and only retention is studied.

Across about 25 queries no paper manipulates the cross-lineage sharing rate and measures retained improver-edit frequency, and none does a Price-equation split of improver-edit selection into direct and product-linked parts. (1) Floor effect. ZMmJDeDTXk and SelfImprove-Bench show improver edits are about 0% even at r=0, so start from a non-zero frequency.

judges.strongest: It speaks directly to the user's question of why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves. It gives a falsifiable, mechanistic answer from another field: shared products break the link between an improver and its fitness. It turns MetaShare's 0/24 self-modification records into a prediction. The manipulated dose (r), the clade-credit contrast, the provenance-stripped control against the scrounging account, and the Price-equation split of direct and indirect selection are the right tools to separate mechanisms. It is cheap on open models.
judges.weakest: As specified, the headline result is close to built in by design. If improver edits are selected through lineage-level harness fitness, and r=1 copies every accepted harness edit into every lineage, then the lineages' harnesses converge. Lineage fitness then cannot tell improvers apart, so suppression follows from the mechanics, not from an empirical law. The surprising part, the quantitative fit of r* = 1 - c/(s_ind·h), cannot be estimated with 8 lineages x 15 generations x 5 seeds. Estimating s_ind, h and c from noisy LLM-edit populations with near-zero base rates will give confidence intervals on r* that cover the whole [0,1] range. Other problems: the floor effect (improver edits about 0% even at r=0), proposal bias versus selection, and clade credit already existing (Looped-RSI, HGM CMP, Group Elite Selection). Together these leave thin novelty and a weak null story.
judges.mustFix: (1) Specify the selection rule for improver edits. They must be accepted through a channel where sharing is not mechanically guaranteed to erase the signal. Otherwise, state in advance the non-trivial part: the functional form and the location of r*. (2) Use a proposal quota or seeded improver variants with known s_ind. Make the main measure retention probability, or the selection coefficient per proposed improver edit, not raw frequency. (3) Estimate s_ind, h and c from the r=0 arm and a cost-manipulation arm, and register the predicted r* before running intermediate r values. Use more r levels (at least 5) and fewer generations if needed, so a threshold can be told apart from a linear decline. (4) Add the provenance-stripped, edit-count-matched sharing arm and report harness-edit retention, to rule out uniform scrounging (2609.38516). (5) Power: aim for at least 8 seeds per arm. Run a power analysis from the pilot variance. Replicate on a second model family, not just a larger Qwen. (6) Give up clade credit as a contribution, and do not claim novelty for the pop-gen framing (Wright-GM, Mendel-GM).
judges.reviewerQuote: The modifier-theory lens is elegant, but at r=1 the lineages share identical harnesses by construction, so of course lineage selection can no longer favor any improver. What the authors would need to show is that the critical sharing rate predicted from independently estimated s_ind, h and c matches the observed one. With 8 lineages, 5 seeds and improver edits that almost never occur, I am not convinced that estimate is identifiable. Clade credit as a remedy is already Looped-RSI/HGM.

judges.strongest: It makes a real, falsifiable, quantitative prediction: a critical sharing rate r* = 1 - c/(s_ind h), set by parameters you can estimate from the r=0 arm. It also gives a mechanistic account of an observed anomaly, MetaShare's 0/24 self-modification records under heavy sharing. That is a rare outcome-agnostic design in a field full of method papers. The Price-equation split of direct and product-linked selection would be a reusable analysis tool for any population-based RSI system, and the sharing rate is a dose knob that is cheap to manipulate.
judges.weakest:
The modifier-theory mapping only holds if selection on improver edits happens at the lineage or population level: lineages reproduce or are replaced according to relative fitness. As written, acceptance is gated per lineage on that lineage's own validation. If an improver edit is kept or dropped by its own lineage's successor quality, sharing harness edits to other lineages never enters that decision, the (1 - r) term is zero by construction, and the null is trivial rather than informative. Several other problems compound this.
- The floor effect: natural improver-edit rates are about 0. The forced-quota fix changes the system being studied.
- The theory is borrowed. Reduction principle, mutator hitchhiking and Group Elite Selection 2204.04817 make it non-novel.
- The rescue arm (clade credit) is already published as Looped-RSI and HGM's CMP.
- With 8 lineages and 5 populations, the Price covariance terms will be dominated by noise. s_ind for LLM improver edits is probably tiny and highly context-dependent, so fitting r* before running the high-r arms is likely to produce confidence intervals spanning [0, 1].

title: The Evolvability Window: Meta-Level Self-Modification Pays Off Only at Intermediate Rates of Real-World Change (a Modularly-Varying-Goals Lens)
claim: Borrowing modularly varying goals from evolutionary biology (Kashtan & Alon 2005, where evolvability evolves only under periodic goal switching that shares subgoals), the claim is that both the frequency of improver-level self-edits and their payoff relative to a fixed improver peak at an intermediate era-switching period T* of about 2 to 4 improver generations. The prediction is an inverted U: the payoff is about zero for very fast switching (noise) and for very slow switching (effectively stationary), and is clearly positive at T*.
alt: Finding that payoff rises monotonically with switching frequency would say that 'more change, more meta-learning' with no fast-switch penalty, so benchmarks should simply maximize churn. Finding that payoff is flat would say that the timescale of the environment does not explain why improvers rarely self-edit. Either result gives harness and benchmark designers a quantitative design rule, and the biology mapping is novel in this literature.
design:
Testbed: the shared Gödel-lite loop with S1–S5, comparing editable-improver arms against fixed-improver arms.

Environment: the real-drift eras from DriftEras (API drift types E1–E3), plus a goal component made of two real task families that share subskills (for example pydantic-based validation and httpx client code over the same real schemas, which is the 'modular' shared structure). The schedule alternates between era states with period T ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, ∞} improver generations, where one generation is one fixed batch of tasks and one improvement step. Reverting changes are included (deprecation, then shim restored), so retention matters.

A modularity control: alternate between two unrelated drift sources that share no subgoals. Biology predicts no evolvability peak in this case.

Matched total compute per lineage. Models: Qwen3-14B and 32B. Six lineages per T per arm (two arms × six T × two modularity conditions).

Metrics:
- improver-edit rate;
- adaptation lag after each switch (generations needed to recover 90% of pre-switch accuracy), which is the biological 'evolvability' readout;
- final held-out accuracy on an unseen fifth era.
Statistics: fit a quadratic in log T and alternatively a piecewise model. The preregistered test is a negative quadratic coefficient with the vertex inside the grid, using the two-lines test (Simonsohn) for the U shape.
law: Payoff(T) ∝ (T/τ_g) · exp(−T/T_s), an inverted U. τ_g is the improver's generation time and T_s is the mean persistence of a meta-rule's usefulness. The peak is at T* = T_s. The prediction is that T* is near 2–4 generations under shared-subgoal (modular) switching, and that there is no interior peak under non-modular switching.
pilot:
Use T ∈ {1, 4, ∞}, the modular condition only, 3 lineages on Qwen3-14B, 2 libraries, and about $20 for drafting tasks (reusing the DriftEras pilot).
Go if the improver-editable arm's lag reduction at T = 4 exceeds the reductions at T = 1 and T = ∞ by at least 1 generation in at least 2 of 3 lineages.
Kill if lag is identical across T (CI overlap at every T). In that case the timescale lens does not bite and should be dropped.
closest: Kashtan & Alon 2005 (PNAS, 'Spontaneous evolution of modularity and network motifs') shows evolvability arising under switching goals, but for biological and neural networks rather than LLM improvers. The Seven-Year Itch 2e5z57jIPK finds a crossover in the length of memory history, not in the switching period of the environment. Continual-ARC 2611.14505 tests dormant return but is stationary and object-level. Metaⁿ 2608.24735 finds that depth stalls, but in stationary settings. I found no LLM prior or concurrent work that sweeps the environment's switching period and compares editable against fixed improvers. The design's core is unclaimed. Three changes would help it survive review:

(1) Biology already owns the inverted-U itself. Kashtan & Alon 2005/2007, Stephens 1991 and Dunlap & Stephens 2009 (learning is favoured at intermediate rates of environmental change) and Bedau & Packard 2003 (evolution of evolvability via mutation rates) all have it. Frame the paper as a test of whether LLM meta-level self-modification obeys that law. The new parts are the measured T* in improver generations and the modular-vs-non-modular dissociation. Cite Lo & Zhao 2611.07048 as the single-shift theory you extend to periodic switching.

(2) Use 2610.25858 as the stream/metric precedent and as a baseline. Its blocked vs interleaved Mix results are the two T endpoints of your sweep. Reuse its plasticity/stability/interference decomposition so adaptation lag is comparable.

(3) Handle the empty-cell risk before anything else. SelfImprove-Bench reports 0% organic improver edits, and Improvement by Inheritance agrees. Run a ≤$50 pilot at T = 2 with Qwen3-32B and measure the organic improver-edit rate. If it is near zero, change the headline from 'edit frequency peaks at T*' to 'payoff of a forced or budgeted improver edit peaks at T*'. Under that design, every lineage must make one improver edit every k generations, and you measure its marginal value against a fixed improver. Report the organic edit rate as a secondary outcome: 'organic self-edit rate does not track T*' is a publishable negative result in its own right.

Also:

judges.strongest: This is the only design I know of that manipulates the environment's switching period as an independent variable and contrasts an editable improver against a fixed one. It gives a direct, mechanistic answer to the mentor's question: why do meta-harnesses rarely update themselves, and when should they? The modular vs non-modular control is the one piece that could turn 'there is a peak' into a real dissociation with a theory behind it.
judges.weakest: The inverted U is close to guaranteed by construction, so the headline result is not very surprising. With T=infinity there is no change to adapt to, and with T=0.5 the eras switch inside a single batch, so no edit made per generation can follow them. Payoff near zero at both ends falls out of the definitions, not out of any law. The proposed law Payoff ∝ (T/τ_g)·exp(−T/T_s) adds nothing as written: T_s is never measured independently, so 'T* = T_s' is fitted after the fact and cannot be falsified. Two further problems: SelfImprove-Bench reports 0% organic improver edits, so the edit-rate DV may be empty in every cell, and the forced-edit fallback changes the claim. Power is also weak: 6 lineages in a two-lines test on a noisy payoff. And the full grid of 144 lineages, where T=8 needs roughly 40 or more generations per lineage, with Qwen3-32B in the mix, is unlikely to fit within $3k of GPU time for a solo undergrad.
judges.mustFix: (1) Measure T_s on its own, before the sweep. One way: take improver edits made in era A, replay them frozen, and record how many generations they keep a positive marginal value. Then preregister T* = T_s as an out-of-sample prediction. That makes the law falsifiable rather than a curve fit. (2) Make the modular vs non-modular dissociation the headline test (a T × modularity interaction), not the U shape itself, because the U is mostly guaranteed by the extreme cells. Drop T=0.5, or justify it as a separate within-batch-mixing condition tied to 2610.25858. (3) Run the ≤$50 organic-edit pilot first. If organic edits are near zero, change the main DV to the marginal value of a forced or budgeted improver edit, and report the organic edit rate as a secondary negative result. (4) Make the cost credible. Use 14B only for the sweep and 32B only for a replication at T* and at the two endpoints, with GPU-hour accounting. Power the lineage count from the pilot's variance, aiming for at least 10 per key cell, and use a smaller grid such as {1, 2, 4, 8, ∞}. (5) Match compute per generation and per lineage across T, and use the same number of switch events, not only the same total compute. Otherwise lineages at large T see fewer switches and the adaptation-lag estimate becomes noisier at that end.
judges.reviewerQuote: The authors find that meta-level self-modification pays off at intermediate switching rates. But that is nearly true by definition: no edit can track switches faster than a generation, and nothing needs tracking in a stationary environment. The paper's own contribution would have to be the predicted location of the peak and the modular/non-modular dissociation. The first is fitted after the fact through an unmeasured T_s, and the second rests on six lineages per cell. I would want T_s estimated independently and the interaction properly powered before I believe the 'law' is anything more than a parameterised curve fit.

judges.strongest: The core manipulation is unclaimed and clean. It sweeps the environment's switching period and compares an editable improver against a fixed one, with a modular vs non-modular control. That gives a dissociation test with a sharp, preregisterable shape prediction (vertex inside the grid, plus Simonsohn two-lines). It also speaks directly to the user's two questions, 'why don't meta-harnesses update themselves' and 'what kind of continual, grounded benchmark forces them to', with a timescale answer rather than another benchmark. The biology framing (Kashtan & Alon, Stephens 1991, Dunlap & Stephens 2009) gives reviewers an established prior to test against, not a vague analogy. 2610.25858's blocked vs Mix results anchor the endpoints for free.
judges.weakest:
Three structural problems.

(a) The empty-cell problem. Organic improver-edit rate is about 0% (SelfImprove-Bench, Improvement-by-Inheritance). So the 'edit-frequency peaks at T*' headline is probably unmeasurable, and the forced or budgeted-edit fallback changes the claim to something weaker.

(b) The 'law' is close to unfalsifiable as written. Payoff ∝ (T/τ_g)·exp(−T/T_s), with T* = T_s fit from the same curve, is circular unless T_s (meta-rule usefulness persistence) is measured independently, for example by re-applying a frozen meta-edit k generations later. The predicted T* of 2–4 generations sits in the middle of a 6-point log grid, so almost any hump 'confirms' it.

(c) Compute and power. 2 arms × 6 T × 2 modularity × 6 lineages × 2 models is about 288 lineages. The T=8 arm needs at least 3–4 periods, so 30+ generations each, on 14B/32B agentic coding loops. That is very tight for $3k and an undergrad. Six noisy lineages per cell is underpowered for a U test. 'Modular' (pydantic+httpx sharing schemas) vs 'non-modular' is a hand-built distinction that reviewers will call arbitrary unless shared-subskill overlap is quantified.

The T=∞ ≈ 0 payoff prediction also conflicts with DGM/ADAS-style stationary gains. If stationary meta-edits help even modestly, the curve is monotone-decreasing, not a U.
judges.mustFix:
1. Before anything else, run the ≤$50 organic-edit-rate pilot at T=2 on Qwen3-32B. If the rate is near 0, make the primary outcome the marginal payoff of a scheduled improver edit (one every k generations) vs a fixed improver, and report organic edit rate as a secondary outcome.

2. Measure T_s independently of the payoff curve. Freeze each meta-edit and re-test its benefit at lags 1..8 generations to get a persistence half-life, then preregister T* = T_s as an out-of-sample prediction. That turns curve-fitting into a test.

3. Cut the design to roughly 2 arms × {0.5,1,2,4,∞} × 2 modularity × 10+ lineages on one model (14B). Use 32B only for the T* and T=∞ replication cells. Power the two-lines test from the pilot variance.

4. Make modularity graded, not binary. Use a measured shared-subskill overlap fraction (for example the fraction of shared test-relevant API symbols), so the prediction is that peak height scales with overlap.

5. Make DriftEras explicitly secondary to the law, and reuse the 2610.25858 plasticity/stability/interference decomposition so adaptation lag is comparable to prior work.
judges.reviewerQuote: The question of when meta-level self-modification pays off as a function of the environment's switching period is new for LLM self-improvers, and the modular/non-modular control is a nice touch borrowed from Kashtan & Alon. However, the 'law' is fit to the same data it claims to predict. T_s is never measured independently. The organic improver-edit rate is near zero in the authors' own setting, so the headline quantity becomes a forced-edit intervention. With six lineages per cell I am not convinced the inverted-U survives proper multiple-comparison control. I would raise my score if T* were predicted out-of-sample from a separately measured meta-rule persistence and the modularity effect were graded rather than binary.

judges.strongest: The modular-vs-non-modular switching control. It turns a curve-fitting exercise into a dissociation test with a mechanism: shared-subgoal switching should produce an interior T* and unrelated switching should not. No LLM self-improvement paper sweeps the environment's switching period against a fixed-improver vs editable-improver contrast. It also fits Yin's Gödel Agent line directly, because it asks when self-referential edits to the improver are worth making at all.
judges.weakest: Two problems: the outcome may not exist, and the budget does not hold. SelfImprove-Bench and Improvement-by-Inheritance both report roughly 0% organic improver edits, so the headline metric (edit rate peaking at T*) will probably be zero in every cell. Forcing edits changes the claim to 'value of a forced meta-edit vs T', which is a weaker and less biological claim. The 'law' Payoff ∝ (T/τ_g)·exp(−T/T_s) is close to circular: its peak is at T_s by construction, and T_s is not measured independently. Compute is also badly underestimated. The design is 2 arms × 6 T × 2 modularity × 6 lineages × 2 models = 288 lineages. Each T = 8 lineage needs at least 3 switches (about 24+ generations), and every generation is a batch of agentic coding tasks plus an improver step. That is far beyond a modest GPU for 32B, and very tight at $3k even with cheap hosted Qwen. With 6 noisy lineages per cell, the Simonsohn two-lines test will probably be underpowered.
judges.mustFix: (1) Before anything else, run a ≤$50 organic-edit pilot at T = 2. If the organic edit rate is below about 5%, preregister the forced/budgeted-edit design (one improver edit every k generations, marginal value against a fixed improver) as the primary outcome, and report the organic edit rate as a secondary result. (2) Estimate T_s independently, as the measured half-life of a meta-rule's usefulness from rollback/ablation of past improver edits. Then predict T* from it before running the sweep, so the law can actually fail. Otherwise drop the functional form and preregister only the inverted U plus the modular dissociation. (3) Cut the scope. Use one model (Qwen3-14B) for the full grid and run 32B only at T ∈ {1, T*, ∞} as a replication. Use the grid T ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 4, ∞} and power the lineages per cell from the pilot variance; expect 10+. Put a cost spreadsheet in the plan. (4) Frame the paper as testing whether LLM meta-level self-modification obeys the known biological law (Kashtan & Alon; Stephens 1991; Dunlap & Stephens 2009). Use 2610.25858 blocked/interleaved as the T endpoints and baseline, and reuse its plasticity/stability decomposition. Make DriftEras a secondary contribution.
judges.reviewerQuote: The modular-vs-non-modular dissociation is a clever import from evolutionary biology, and I have not seen it tested on LLM improvers. However, the stated 'law' peaks at T_s by construction and T_s is never measured independently. Most cells report improver edits that had to be forced. As a result, the paper shows at most that a mandated meta-edit's value depends weakly on switching period in one testbed with six seeds, which falls short of a law.

title: DriftEras: Real Library-History Eras Whose Drift *Type* Changes Make Improver Self-Edits Necessary, Not Optional
claim: On a stream built from real post-cutoff Python library releases, where each era brings a different drift type (deprecation with a warning shim, then silent semantic change, then hard removal), a Gödel-lite loop that may edit its own improver procedure ends with at least 10 pp higher held-out success than a matched-compute fixed-improver loop. On a control stream that uses the same real changes but keeps one drift type throughout, the gap is under 2 pp.
alt: If the improver-editable arm does not beat the fixed improver even when the drift type switches, the 'improvers never self-edit' finding (SelfImprove-Bench 0%, Improvement by Inheritance) is a capability gap, not an incentive gap. That would be the first real-data evidence for it, and it changes what the field should build: improver-edit training or scaffolds rather than better benchmarks. Either outcome ships a reusable, time-split, certified real-drift benchmark, which the review shows does not exist.
law: Predicted interaction: Δ(c − b) ≈ β · (number of drift-type switches seen), with β > 0 on the type-switching stream and β ≈ 0 on the control stream. Secondary prediction: improver-edit rate rises with stale-rule harm in the preceding era.
pilot:
Use 2 libraries (pydantic v1→v2→v2.x semantic changes, httpx), 3 eras, 25 tasks per era, arms (a) and (c), 3 lineages, Qwen3-32B local plus at most $40 of API calls for task drafting.
Go if both hold: (1) at least 70% of drafted tasks pass certification, and the old-era idiom fails on at least 80% of certified tasks; (2) in E2 the fixed-improver arm keeps applying an E1 rule that is now wrong on at least 20% of tasks. Without (2), object-level adaptation is not being stressed.
Kill if (c) never edits S4/S5 even after the E2 failures and also does not beat (a), and a manual check shows the S4 edit interface itself works. In that case pivot to the capability-gap framing.
closest: Δτ-Bench 2610.34238 uses synthetic, capability-preserving tool transforms and only object-level skill methods; the delta here is real releases plus a change in drift type. Are-SE-CL 2610.25858 builds synthetic block streams with a fixed evolver; the delta is that the improver itself varies. MemDev-Bench 2610.27524 has a real, time-valid pipeline but is memory-only, with no improver and no change in drift type. check.reposition:
I found no paper that makes this exact claim: that switching drift type on a real library-release stream is the condition under which letting the improver edit itself beats a fixed improver, with the arm×stream interaction as the preregistered test. Every component has a close neighbour, though. The paper needs repositioning to survive:

(1) Present it as "when does editing the improver pay?", an environmental-necessity account that competes with VERSE's verification account. Cross S4 with verification availability (with/without execution replay) in a 2x2, so the result separates non-stationarity from verification as the cause.

(2) Cite Are-SE-CL as the source of the stream design, including its compound and Mix control. The new parts are the S4 arm, real post-cutoff releases, and the drift-type variable. Do not claim "drift-typed streams" or the "mixed control" as contributions.

(3) Add Harness^2-style harnessing-level recursion and a MetaEvoForge-style evolved improver as baseline arms. The forward-transfer-of-improver metric is then a test across time-ordered eras, not across tasks.

(4) Take the drift taxonomy from ReScopeBench and AgentDriftBench, and the silent-semantic-change task source from Update from Hell. Measure stale-rule harm as ReScopeBench measures update coverage.

(5) The biggest empirical risk: improvers rarely edit themselves (SelfImprove-Bench, Improvement by Inheritance). The 10 pp target is aggressive. Pilot one switch (E1 to E2) first. Preregister a smaller effect plus the edit-rate prediction (improver edits rise after stale-rule harm). That prediction is the most novel and least scooped piece, so consider leading with it if the accuracy gap is small.

(6) Drop the "law" framing unless at least 3 switch counts are tested. With four eras there are at most 3 switches, so β is close to unidentifiable.

title: A Reach–Discoverability Law for Meta-Harness Openness: Optimal Search-Space Openness Grows with Evaluation Budget and Task Drift
claim: The held-out gain from harness search is inverted-U in edit-surface openness L0–L4. The openness that maximizes gain, o*, increases with the log of the evaluation budget and with the task drift rate. On a stationary stream at budgets of 500 rollouts or fewer, prompt+memory (L1) beats improver-editable (L4). Under drift at budgets of 4k rollouts or more, L3/L4 beats L1 by at least 5 held-out points.
alt: If gain rises monotonically with openness at every budget, then constraint is pure loss, which contradicts the RRSI, SelfImprove-Bench and Inheritance findings, and the result would be a strong 'just open it up' paper. If gain falls monotonically, then openness is a trap, and the paper becomes a quantitative argument for constrained harness search. Both outcomes come with a fitted functional form and a released sweep.
design: MetaLite with 5 nested openness levels. Openness is measured two ways: the nominal level, and the empirical log-size of the reachable edit space, estimated by the proposal entropy of the unfiltered proposer over 200 draws. A third dimension, 'disposition openness' (the Values-Shape 'openness' statement on or off), is added to separate the two variables that papers conflate. Grid: 5 levels × 4 budgets (250, 500, 1k, 4k rollouts) × 2 streams × 5 seeds. Stationary stream: LiveBench-Math plus τ-bench-lite. Drift stream: VersionShift, built from real library churn, i.e. tasks requiring pandas 1.x→2.x, numpy 1→2, pydantic 1→2 and sklearn API changes, sourced from CodeUpdateArena/VersiCode-style changelog items and executed in pinned containers so that the failures that matter move from prompt-addressable to tool/runtime-addressable. That is about 200 runs of a small local task agent (Qwen3-8B) with a local proposer (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B). API is used only for an annotator. Controls: the same proposer and selection gate (a paired 2σ activation gate taken from HarnessBank, held fixed) at every level, and a random-edit arm at each level to separate reach from proposer skill. Metrics: held-out accuracy after a fixed budget, gain per rollout, generalization gap (search minus held-out) and pass@k. Fit the law with hierarchical nonlinear regression and test predictions on a held-out budget (8k) and a held-out task (LiveCodeBench-lite) before looking at them.
law: G(o,B) = R(o) · [1 − exp(−B·q / S(o))] − λ·S(o)/n_val. R(o) is the reach: the fraction of failure mass whose cause is editable at openness o. It is measured by an oracle-localized fix probe. S(o) is the effective search-space size, measured by proposal entropy. q is the proposer hit rate. The last term is the overfitting penalty from validation size n_val. Implied optimum: o* is where R'(o)/R(o) = S'(o)/S(o)·(B q / S(o))·..., so o* rises with log B. Drift raises R for high o, which moves o* to the right.
pilot: Week 1: L0, L1, L3 and L4 only, 2 budgets (250, 1k), the VersionShift-mini drift stream with 60 tasks, 2 seeds. About 32 runs on local GPU and under $30 API. Go if the ranking of levels flips between the two budgets, or between stationary and drift, by more than seed SD for at least one pair. Kill if L1 dominates at every budget and stream with no crossover, which would mean the proposer cannot use higher surfaces at all. In that case, fold the work into idea 1 as evidence about 'reach'.
closest: EvoSpace (MQoRwlss2y): progressively expands edit space, but fits no law and has no budget×drift sweep. SelfImprove-Bench (2611.02797): a generalization ladder, not an openness sweep. HarnessBank (2607.13683): QD over levers, single budget. Harness-MAP (HM48DQvAqS): structure-token factorization for search efficiency, not openness vs efficacy. RRSI/Metaⁿ (ctx): report that wider scope or more depth stalls or overfits, with no functional form. What is new here: a falsifiable two-factor law, with reach and discoverability measured separately, plus a drift benchmark grounded in real library churn that predicts when openness pays.

title: Why Meta-Harnesses Don't Edit Themselves: It's the Credit Horizon, Not the Permission, and Delayed Successor Credit Beats Edit Quotas
claim: Improvers rarely edit themselves mainly because keep-if-better pays an improver edit only one generation later. Giving improver edits delayed successor-quality credit, computed by nested replay, raises both improver-edit rate and held-out successor quality. Structurally forcing improver edits with a quota raises the edit rate but not successor quality.
alt: If quotas improve successor quality as much as delayed credit does, the bottleneck is exploration or salience, not credit assignment. That is an important design result: cheap forcing works, and the scheduling literature (EvoSpace/DyScope) should add mandatory meta-steps. If neither arm improves successor quality while both raise edit rate, the improver is not a productive edit target at this capability. That generalizes Improvement by Inheritance's 'one-shot evidence-routing' finding into a causal negative that tells the field to stop paying for L4 permissions.
law: Credit-horizon model: P(improver edit) ∝ exp(β·E[Δ_immediate]) under keep-if-better. Since E[Δ_immediate | improver edit] ≈ 0, the rate is ≈ 0 regardless of permission. Under delayed credit it is ∝ exp(β·E[Δ_successor]). The prediction: successor-quality gain scales with corr(imp@k credit, held-out successor quality), so a sufficiently noisy replay credit erases A4's advantage. This is tested by varying k ∈ {1,3}.
pilot: Week 1, about $50. Run A0, A3 and A4 × 3 lineages × 8 generations on the CO-Bench subset. Go if (i) A0 improver-edit rate is under 10%, reproducing the SelfImprove-Bench/Inheritance finding in our loop, (ii) A4 raises it above 20%, and (iii) the nested-replay successor-quality metric has a seed SD under half the A0-vs-best-arm difference on at least one task. Kill if A0 already edits the improver at over 25%: the phenomenon does not reproduce, so the work pivots to behavioral analysis only. Also kill if the replay metric is too noisy to rank arms.
closest: Improvement by Inheritance ZMmJDeDTXk (measures successor quality and finds that improvers almost never self-edit, but intervenes on neither credit nor forcing). SelfImprove-Bench 2611.02797 (a forced improver-target arm on one game in one run, with no successor-quality metric). Hyperagents 2603.19461 (permission only). Metaⁿ 2608.24735 (avoids improver editing altogether). MetaSkill-Evolve 2607.05297 (two-timescale updates, but no credit-horizon test or forcing comparison). check.reposition:
No paper found makes the causal claim itself: that improvers rarely edit themselves because of the credit horizon rather than permission or salience. The same goes for the factorial that pits a quota against delayed credit (plus salience and values arms) on successor quality, and for the behavioral codebook of target-choice rationales. The A4 mechanism is not new, though. Replaying improver edits from frozen archive states and accepting them on child gain is essentially IFR (eIJH6HV9LZ). Adopting an improver only when its children are better is RSI-Harness's outer-loop gate (EOrtreQLbv). Delayed descendant credit is HGM/Gödel Ecology clade metaproductivity. Improvement by Inheritance already shows one intervention that raises successor quality.

To survive:
(1) Retitle as a diagnosis paper, e.g. "Why improvers don't edit themselves: a causal decomposition." Present A4 as IFR/CMP-style credit, with an IFR arm and an RSI-Harness-style dual-loop arm, not as a new method.
(2) Make the headline the dissociation: forcing raises the edit rate but not successor quality, while credit raises both. Add a direct test of the credit-horizon law: manipulate E[Δ_immediate | improver edit] by injecting an immediate bonus with no successor content. This placebo-credit arm should raise the edit rate without raising quality, and it separates "pays later" from "pays at all."
(3) Address the RSI-Harness counterexample: its always-forced outer loop does improve the improver. Explain whether that comes from the credit attached to the forcing, and test it with a quota-plus-immediate-gate vs quota-plus-delayed-gate cell (A3 vs A5 already approximates this, so state it explicitly).
(4) Pre-register the k ∈ {1, 3} noise prediction and add k = 5 or a noised replay to trace a dose-response for corr(credit, true successor quality). That curve is the law and is unclaimed.
(5) Keep the behavioral codebook as a co-headline: no one has coded proposers' stated reasons for avoiding the improver. Validate it with κ and link the codes to the arms, e.g. whether salience shifts the "unaware" codes while credit shifts the "low payoff" codes.
(6) Cite LRSI, SelfLineage and EvoTrace. Add 2+ lineages per arm if budget allows, because the A4 vs A3 contrast at n = 6 is fragile.

judges.strongest: The paper is framed as a diagnosis, and that framing is still unclaimed. It is a factorial that dissociates edit rate from successor quality, with arms for permission, salience, values, quota and credit. It scores them with nested-replay successor quality on a sealed held-out family and pairs this with a kappa-validated codebook of the proposer's rationales. If quota works, the scheduling literature should add forced meta-steps. If nothing works, L4 permissions are not worth paying for. Either way the result is publishable. Relevance to self-referential and meta-agent research is very high.
judges.weakest: The causal mechanism is underspecified, and it is confounded with the treatment. The proposer is an LLM that is not trained, so changing the acceptance rule cannot change P(propose improver edit) through any exp(beta*E[delta]) policy. It can only change it if the proposer is told the rule or sees in-context archive feedback about which edits got kept. That makes A4 partly a salience/instruction manipulation, and "edit rate" mixes proposal rate with acceptance rate. Delayed credit mechanically accepts more improver edits even if proposals do not change. Separately, the A4 mechanism itself is already IFR/RSI-Harness/HGM-CMP, so novelty rests entirely on the dissociation and the codebook. The design also has n=6 lineages and a single main optimizer model. Nested replay from 3 archive states over 20 generations on tau2/AppWorld will likely blow through $3k, or the GPU-hours a solo undergrad has, under matched-token accounting.
judges.mustFix: (1) Report proposal rate and acceptance rate separately. State exactly what information about the acceptance rule and past credit reaches the proposer's context in each arm. Add a "rule-disclosed but immediate gate" control and a "delayed gate but rule undisclosed" control, so that credit (selection) is separated from belief about credit (instruction). Without these the credit-horizon law is untestable. (2) Add the placebo immediate-bonus arm and an explicit RSI-Harness-style quota+delayed-gate cell (A5). Frame A4 as IFR/CMP credit, not as a new method. (3) Pre-register the noise-dose curve, using k in {1,3,5} plus injected replay noise against corr(credit, held-out successor quality). That curve is the only novel 'law'. (4) Budget the work honestly: cap the noisy task to a small subset or drop it, raise lineages to 8 or more on the main contrast, and run a power analysis from the pilot SD. (5) Add a second open optimizer family, not just a 2-arm frontier-mini replication.

title: Prior-Subtracted Edit Ledgers: Measuring What Meta-Agents Do Because of Evidence, and Building a Proposer That Only Does That
claim: Across 3 open harness optimizers (GEPA-lite, AHE-lite, Gödel-lite), fewer than half of retained edits in every edit type except runtime/control-flow have higher probability under true evidence than under shuffled evidence. An Evidence-Contrastive Proposer (ECP) that keeps only candidates whose likelihood ratio true:shuffled is at least tau, and that allocates proposal budget by edit type in proportion to measured held-out efficacy divided by propensity, improves held-out score per 100 evaluations by at least 25% relative over the best of the 3 baselines at matched compute.
alt: Suppose most edits do turn out to be evidence-directed once you control for the prior, and ECP does not beat the baselines. That would overturn the DGM null result from 2610.14662 for harness systems. The finding would be that directedness depends on the system, which is publishable as a calibration of the MOT/'Opinionated Optimizers' claims. The released prior-subtracted ledger, the first one for harness systems, still stands as a contribution.
design: Shared testbed MetaLite: a Gödel-lite/Meta-Harness-lite loop with a configurable editable surface. Levels are L0 prompt, L1 +memory/few-shot, L2 +tool/helper code, L3 +control-flow graph, L4 +improver prompt/code. Task agent: Qwen3-8B/Qwen3.5-9B on vLLM, run locally. Proposer: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B served locally, plus one cheap API model (DeepSeek-V3.x) to check generality. Tasks: LiveBench-Math, a τ-bench-retail-style tool task and LiveCodeBench-lite, each split into search, validation and held-out sets. Phase 1 (ledger): replay each baseline over 5 seeds. At every step, sample K=8 proposals under each of 4 conditions: true evidence, evidence shuffled across tasks, null evidence (score only), and evidence from the wrong target failure. An LLM coder validated on 200 human labels classifies each proposal into a unified 7-type schema mapped onto SelfImprove-Bench, EvoTrace and Treude: prompt-add, prompt-delete, memory, tool, control-flow, gate, improver. Directedness per type = P(type, target-hit | true) − P(type | shuffled). For a stratified sample of 400 edits, held-out efficacy comes from single-edit knockouts and add-backs, and activation rate comes from instrumentation. Phase 2 (system): ECP scores each candidate by the proposer's own log-likelihood under true vs shuffled evidence, which is cheap with local models, and filters on that score. It then samples edit types from the efficacy/propensity price list. Arms: ECP, each baseline, ECP without the filter, ECP without the price list, and a prior-only arm where the proposer gets null evidence plus selection. All arms get the same evaluation budget (number of rollouts) and the same proposer-token cap. Metrics: held-out accuracy, held-out gain per evaluation, pass@1 and pass@16 (to check elicitation vs expansion), inert-edit rate and harness length. Stats: 5 seeds × 3 tasks, paired bootstrap CIs, same-start matched-budget swap test as recommended by 2610.27610.
law: Efficacy_type ≈ α · Directedness_type · Reach_type. Reach is the fraction of failures whose editable cause lies inside that surface. Prediction: proposal share should be proportional to D·R, and the observed share is roughly proportional to the prior P_null(type).
pilot: Week 1, GEPA-lite only, LiveBench-Math, 2 seeds × 15 steps × 4 evidence conditions × K=8 proposals, local Qwen proposer, about $20 API for a coder sanity check. Go if the type distributions under true vs shuffled evidence differ for at least one edit type (chi-square p<0.01) and the likelihood-ratio filter, applied post hoc, would have removed at least 30% of the accepted edits that are inert on held-out. Kill if true and shuffled distributions cannot be told apart for every type and post-hoc filtering does not change held-out gain. In that case, pivot to writing the null result up as 'harness optimizers are prior-driven'.
closest: Opinionated Optimizers/MOT (LhhLpXBFgo): diagnoses proposer priors but has no prior subtraction and no fix. Does Failure Feedback Direct Self-Modification (2610.14662): randomized directedness test, but only on DGM logs, per failure rather than per edit type, with no system. SelfImprove-Bench (2611.02797): propensities only. EvoTrace (a2ZN4PGsoR): frequency vs efficacy for program evolution, not harnesses, and no evidence-shuffling. RB-Prompt (uVKMqFVBDG) and HarnessBank (2607.13683): debiasing restricted to length or QD cells. What is new here: a causal prior-vs-evidence decomposition per edit type, done counterfactually, and then a proposer whose filter and budget come directly from that decomposition.

closestFound.summary: A randomized-target directedness test (e-values) on 145 DGM self-modifications finds no target-specific repair (OR 0.69). check.reposition:
I found no paper that does the full package: counterfactual prior subtraction per edit type, across several optimizers, feeding a likelihood-ratio filter and a type-level budget. Most of the pieces are taken, though, so the idea survives only as a system-plus-mechanism paper.

(1) Drop the 'Law' as a novelty claim. Efficacy ≈ α·D·Reach is essentially Eq. 6/7 of 2610.14662 (editable-cause share π_e, proposer prior q_e, breakage). Recast it as a pre-registered quantitative test of that model across edit types and optimizers. 'The He-model predicts per-type efficacy out of sample (R² on held-out tasks)' is a contribution; restating it is not.

(2) Lead with ECP as the method. The novel object is the proposer's own log-likelihood ratio under true vs shuffled evidence, a PMI/contrastive-decoding-style filter applied to edits. Show it beats the obvious neighbours: IDM/Predict-Before-You-Modify (ZBxV5bEYUH) as a pre-evaluation filter, CIG (GhghP7h0cq), a cheap 'evidence-citation' LLM-judge filter, and simple rejection by edit-type quota (prior subtraction without likelihoods).

(3) Run everything inside parent-inheritance loops and count evaluations, not proposer tokens. 2610.41157 shows that inheritance absorbs disclosure effects and that gating and validation dominate cost, so ECP's win has to come from fewer wasted evaluations. Report evaluations-to-target as the primary metric.

(4) Add a wrong-feedback/Melcer-style arm and a 'feedback from another failure family' arm, matching 2610.14662, so reviewers can't say the shuffle condition is novel-but-weak.

(5) Lower the bar on the headline number. 2610.14662 finds 8-step loops ≈ GEPA, and HDA/RSI-Tax show small residual gains, so a ≥25% relative gain per 100 evaluations is high-risk. Pre-register a smaller effect (for example ≥10%) plus a strong secondary claim: ECP cuts inert/breaking edits and harness bloat.

(6) Read the Opinionated Optimizers (LhhLpXBFgo) full PDF before freezing. If MOT already breaks prior-driven proposals down by strategy type, position the ledger as its counterfactual, causal upgrade and use MOT runs as a replay source if they are released.

judges.strongest: The Evidence-Contrastive Proposer turns a diagnostic into a cheap, testable mechanism. It filters edits with the proposer's own log-likelihood ratio under true vs shuffled evidence (a PMI / contrastive-decoding idea applied to harness edits), and with local open models that ratio costs almost nothing. The matched-budget arms are well chosen: no filter, no price list, and a prior-only arm with selection. Pass@1 vs pass@16 separates eliciting what the model already does from expanding it. The L4 improver-directedness row ties straight into Gödel Agent and answers the user's question of why meta-harnesses rarely update themselves. If ECP raises improver-edit share on evidence, that is a concrete answer to 'make it structurally update itself more'.
judges.weakest: Novelty is thin and the scope is too big. The diagnostic, the shuffled and wrong-family evidence controls, and the 'Law' are largely 2610.14662 (Eq. 6/7). The headline 'agents edit from priors' belongs to Opinionated Optimizers/MOT, and the qualitative per-mechanism split belongs to Treude & Baltes. That leaves ECP plus a multi-optimizer, per-type ledger. Meanwhile one undergrad would have to run 3 optimizers × 3 tasks × 5 seeds × 4-6 evidence conditions × K=8, plus 400 knockout/add-back edits, an LLM coder validated on 200 human labels, and a Phase 2 with 6+ arms and new IDM/CIG baselines. That is 2-3 papers of work on a single GPU budget. There is also an unaddressed confound. A true:shuffled likelihood ratio rewards lexical copying of task-specific tokens from the evidence. An edit that quotes the failing example scores a high LR whether or not it is causally useful, so the filter may select surface-specific overfitting edits that look 'directed', which is the exact opposite of what is wanted on held-out. The directedness formula is also not well-formed: P(type, target-hit | true) − P(type | shuffled) mixes a joint and a marginal.
judges.mustFix: (1) Cut scope. Use 2 optimizers (Gödel-lite with L0-L4 surfaces plus GEPA-lite), 2 tasks, 5 seeds, and a 150-edit knockout sample. Drop DeepSeek, or keep it only as a single generality run. (2) Control the lexical-copy confound in the LR filter. Add a shuffle that matches length and n-gram overlap (evidence from a same-category task with paraphrased surface form). Compare ECP against an 'evidence-overlap' heuristic filter, and report LR vs held-out efficacy calibration (AUROC) before using LR as a gate. (3) Present the Law as a pre-registered out-of-sample test of the He-model (2610.14662), predicting per-type held-out efficacy with an R² target. Do not claim it as new. Fix the D definition to be the same quantity under both conditions. (4) Make evaluations-to-target inside parent-inheritance loops the primary metric. Pre-register a gain of at least 10%, with inert/breaking-edit rate and harness bloat as co-primary secondary metrics. Include IDM and a type-quota rejection baseline. (5) Read the MOT full PDF before freezing claims. (6) The pilot must also check LR-vs-efficacy correlation, not only chi-square differences in type distributions, because type distributions will almost certainly differ trivially.
judges.reviewerQuote: The diagnostic half of this paper re-runs 2610.14662's evidence-swap design at a finer grain, and the 'law' is their Eq. 6/7. The contribution therefore rests entirely on ECP. The authors never show that a high true:shuffled likelihood ratio means an edit is causally grounded rather than just copying tokens from the evidence. Without a calibration of LR against held-out efficacy and an overlap-matched control, the reported gains could come from selecting edits that overfit the search split. Gains of around 10% over GEPA-lite on 8B task agents, with five seeds, are unlikely to separate from the baselines.

judges.strongest: The paper's one new piece is ECP itself: a filter based on the proposer's own log-likelihood ratio under true vs shuffled evidence (pointwise mutual information, PMI), applied to harness edits. It is cheap with local open models and gives an operational, testable definition of "evidence-directed" that links the diagnostic to a fix. Every closest neighbour stops at one side: MOT, 2610.14662 and Treude are diagnosis only, while IDM and CIG are fixes with no prior subtraction. The L4 improver row speaks directly to the near-zero improver-edit propensity seen in Gödel-style systems. That gives strong mentor fit and a clear failure story. A null result ("harness optimizers are prior-driven, and filtering doesn't help") is still a usable calibration result.
judges.weakest: Novelty is thin and the scope is too big for one undergrad. 2610.14662 already has the evidence-swap counterfactual and essentially the D·Reach law. MOT holds the headline claim. Treude has the per-mechanism qualitative split. 2610.41157 predicts that parent inheritance absorbs disclosure effects. What remains is a filter plus a budget heuristic, and it has an unexamined confound: PMI under true vs shuffled evidence rewards edits that copy distinctive tokens from the trace verbatim (task IDs, error strings, tool names) and does not reward causally useful edits. So the filter could select for overfit or lexically anchored edits, and may raise inert-edit rates on held-out. On load, Phase 1 alone is 3 optimizers × 5 seeds × 3 tasks × steps × 4–6 evidence conditions × K=8. Add 400 knockout/add-back evaluations, a 200-item human-label coder validation, and Phase 2 with about 9 arms including reimplemented IDM and CIG. That is not feasible in 6 months for one person with a 30B proposer and an 8B agent on a ≤$3k budget. The ≥25% headline effect is also implausible given 8-step≈GEPA and RSI-Tax.

judges.strongest: The Evidence-Contrastive Proposer is a real method that nobody has published yet. It scores each proposed edit by the proposer's own log-likelihood under true evidence versus shuffled evidence, which is a PMI-style filter. It is cheap with local open models and testable at matched evaluation budget. If it beats IDM/CIG-style pre-evaluation filters on evaluations-to-target, that is a clean, reusable result, and the improver (L4) directedness row ties directly to the Gödel Agent line.

title: The Drift Barrier of Harness Evolution: Evaluation-Set Size Is Effective Population Size, and Kimura's Fixation Law Predicts Scaffolding Bloat
claim: Inert and slightly harmful harness components (phantom guards, never-firing checks, redundant instructions) accumulate at a rate set by the selection gate's effective population size N_e = number of paired validation tasks divided by the per-task score variance. As N_e grows, accumulated inert length falls along the curve predicted by Kimura's fixation probability. A cheap 'N_e-boosting' gate, which uses paired, variance-reduced evaluation and a length cost scaled by 1/N_e, cuts harness length by at least 40% with no loss in held-out accuracy.
alt: If bloat does not depend on N_e and is instead set only by the proposer's add rate (the phantom-guardrail q), then bloat is a mutation-bias phenomenon and not a drift phenomenon. The remedy is then on the proposer side (RB-Prompt, idea 1), not on the gate side. Either result settles which side of the 'proposer vs selection' debate controls bloat, using a quantitative test borrowed from population genetics.
design: This applies Lynch's mutational-hazard / drift-barrier hypothesis from evolutionary biology, which explains why genomes bloat in small populations, to harness search. MetaLite at L0–L2 with an add-only proposer and with an add+delete proposer. Sweep the gate's validation size n ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} tasks, and noise level via agent temperature, so that N_e covers more than an order of magnitude. Use 6 seeds per cell on LiveBench-Math and τ-bench-lite, and evaluate held-out on separate tasks. Instrument every component for activation (does it fire) and measure its selection coefficient s by leave-one-out on a large audit set of 500 tasks run once at the end. Measured quantities: insertion rate u per type, distribution of fitness effects (DFE) per edit surface (deleterious, neutral and beneficial fractions; gamma fit), fixation rate of components with s≈0 and s<0, and final harness length and inert fraction. Prediction test: plug the measured u and DFE into Kimura's P_fix(s, N_e) to predict steady-state inert length for each n before running the large-n cells, then compare. Intervention arm: an N_e-boosting gate with paired common-random-number evaluation, control variates from a frozen reference agent, and a length cost c(ℓ) = κ/N_e. Compare to a HarnessBank-style 2σ gate and a Masked-Erosion leave-one-out gate at matched rollouts. Stats: mixed-effects regression of inert length on log N_e, and calibration of predicted vs observed fixation.
law: P_fix(s) = (1 − e^{−2s}) / (1 − e^{−4 N_e s}). Here s is the true held-out effect divided by the per-task score SD, and N_e is the effective number of paired validation tasks. Expected inert load is roughly u_neutral · T · P_fix(0≈1/N_e scaling) + Σ_{s<0} u_s · T · P_fix(s). Prediction: the drift barrier is at |s| ≈ 1/(2N_e), so components with effect below that threshold accumulate as if neutral.
pilot: Week 1: GEPA-lite with an add-only proposer on LiveBench-Math, n ∈ {8, 32, 128}, 3 seeds, 30 steps, local Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-Coder, under $15 API. Go if final inert-component count drops monotonically with n, with the n=8 vs n=128 difference larger than 2 seed SDs, and if the measured DFE has a substantial near-neutral mass (at least 30% of edits with |s| below 0.5 SD). Kill if inert count is flat across n. In that case report the mutation-bias finding and merge into idea 1's subtractive-operator arm.
closest: Phantom Guardrails (2607.13083): add-only ratchet with a fixed entry rate q; does not vary the gate population size or model fixation. Masked Erosion (2610.38392): gate statistics determine which deletions survive; no fixation law and no DFE. HarnessBank (2607.13683): reports that removing the 2σ gate produces phantom progress, but there is no N_e sweep. RB-Prompt (uVKMqFVBDG): length penalty on the proposer side. Auditing Harness Evolution (yl1XFtnTn4): reports inert guards. Mutation Without Variation (2606.05408): proposer attractors without selection. What is new here: importing population-genetic theory (Kimura fixation, the Lynch drift barrier, DFE estimation) to give a quantitative, predictive account of bloat as a function of evaluation budget, plus a gate derived from that theory. Scoop checks on S2 and ICLR27 found no prior work.

closestFound.id: arXiv 2610.38392 (Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents)
closestFound.title: Masked Erosion
closestFound.summary: Section 3.3 'Drift and Selection' borrows Kimura (1968) and Ohta (1973) and defines a standardized effect z = g·sqrt(n)/σ. This is effectively the proposal's s·sqrt(N_e), with σ the SD of the paired per-task difference. It predicts P_accept ≈ Φ(z) for greedy gates and Φ(z − z_α) for paired gates. Batch size is swept (n = 20, 40, 120), and a gate simulator frozen before the loops predicts where protection breaks as a function of edit cost and batch size. Gates compared: paired McNemar, greedy, split-half, veto, audit, and margin-aware leave-one-out. The appendix measures how often no-op edits are accepted: 0.40 greedy, 0.32 split-half, 0.013 paired.
closestFound.overlap: High on the framework, low on the target. It already imports drift-vs-selection language, sweeps gate n, and validates a pre-registered acceptance law, which takes away the proposal's 'what is new: importing population-genetic theory' pitch. It studies deletion of costly safeguards, finding that a larger n admits cheaper deletions. It does not study insertion and accumulation of inert components (bloat), harness length, a DFE, or a Kimura P_fix curve. Its no-op acceptance data also undercut the proposal's law (see reposition).

closestFound.title: Phantom Guardrails: When Self-Improving Agent Harnesses Fix Failures That Never Happened
closestFound.summary: Inert guards for failures that never occur enter an add-only accept loop at a per-round rate q = 0.05 and never leave. Accept-if-not-worse ratchets them in, strict improvement lets them ride along with real fixes, and warrant-aware acceptance excludes them. In a prune-capable loop, persistence depends on the proposer's parsimony: a second look removes the phantom 88% of the time.
closestFound.overlap: It covers the phenomenon (inert guards ratcheting in under add-only proposers, with the gate rule deciding persistence) and the add-only vs add+delete contrast. It does not vary gate size, model fixation, or measure a DFE.

check.reposition:
Problems to fix before this survives review:
(1) The Kimura P_fix law is the wrong model for these loops. Harness search is a single-lineage elitist hill-climber, not a Wright–Fisher population. For a truly inert component (s = 0), the acceptance probability does not scale as 1/N_e; it is set by the gate's tie rule and stays flat as n grows. Masked Erosion's appendix measures no-op acceptance at 0.40 (greedy), 0.32 (split-half) and 0.013 (paired). Its own model is P_acc ≈ Φ(s·sqrt(n)/σ − z_gate). So 'inert length falls along Kimura's curve as N_e grows' is likely falsified for zero-cost junk. Bloat only responds to n for components with a real small cost: context dilution, tokens, latency.
(2) The 'importing population genetics' pitch is gone. Masked Erosion already invokes Kimura/Ohta drift vs selection, sweeps gate n, and validates pre-registered break points.
(3) '≥40% shorter, no loss' is already shown post hoc by SHarP. Length-cost gates exist: RB-Prompt, CoEvolve. Paired CRN plus control-variate evaluation exists: EvalAlloc.

What survives is the insertion/accumulation side, plus the first measured distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of LLM proposer edits per edit surface. Reposition as 'The Two-Sided Drift Barrier of Gated Harness Search':
- Derive the correct single-lineage acceptance and stationary-load law: L*(n, σ, gate, u_add/u_del, DFE), with the barrier at |s| ≈ z_gate·σ/sqrt(n).
- Predict both halves from that one law: bloat (cheap junk inserted, sitting below the barrier) and erosion (cheap safeguards deleted, Masked Erosion's result). The non-obvious, falsifiable prediction is that raising n reduces slightly harmful bloat but increases erosion of cheap safeguards. Exactly-inert components respond to the gate's tie rule, not to n.
- Make the measured per-surface DFE (gamma fit; deleterious, neutral and beneficial fractions over prompt, memory, tool and code edits) and out-of-sample prediction of final length on real optimizers (GEPA, ACE, Meta-Harness-style loops) the headline contribution.
- Treat the gate as an ablation, not the contribution. Baselines at matched rollouts: Masked Erosion's paired and margin-aware gates, SHarP post-hoc pruning, RB-Prompt's length penalty, TRUST/SGM, and EvalAlloc-style CRN.
- Cite Masked Erosion as the closest prior work up front, and the GP bloat literature (Langdon & Poli: introns, 'fitness causes bloat', the removal-bias and drift theories of bloat), which reviewers will raise.

4. Shrink the grid. Use one benchmark plus one transfer benchmark, n in {8, 32, 128}, 2 proposers, and at least 5 seeds. Do the leave-one-out audit on a stratified subsample of components to fit a $3k budget, and show results on at least 2 model families.
judges.reviewerQuote: The population-genetics framing is attractive but misapplied. A single-lineage hill-climber with a significance gate does not obey Kimura's fixation law, and the authors' own closest prior work (Masked Erosion) already shows that no-op acceptance is set by the tie rule, not by n. What would interest me is the measured DFE of LLM edits, and the prediction that larger gates trade bloat for safeguard erosion. Rebuild the paper around those.

judges.strongest: The repositioned version makes one prediction that can fail: raising gate n should cut slightly harmful bloat and at the same time increase erosion of cheap safeguards, while exactly-inert junk should respond only to the gate's tie rule. That claim is non-obvious. The other strong part is the first measured distribution of fitness effects (DFE) for LLM proposer edits, broken out by edit surface (prompt, memory, tool, code) and fit with a gamma. That would be a reusable empirical artifact that no 2026 paper provides. Both outcomes are publishable: if bloat tracks n, it is a drift barrier; if it tracks only the add rate, it is mutation bias, which settles the proposer-vs-selection debate.
judges.weakest: The pitch as written is partly scooped and partly wrong. Masked Erosion (2610.38392) already brings drift-vs-selection language into this area, already sweeps gate n, and already validates a pre-registered acceptance law, so 'importing population genetics' is not new. More seriously, Kimura's P_fix assumes a Wright-Fisher population, and these loops are single-lineage elitist hill-climbers. For s=0, acceptance is set by the tie rule, not by 1/N_e. Masked Erosion's own no-op acceptance rates (0.40 greedy, 0.32 split-half, 0.013 paired) contradict the headline curve. The '>=40% shorter, no accuracy loss' intervention is not new either: SHarP already shows it post hoc, RB-Prompt and CoEvolve already use length costs, and EvalAlloc already uses CRN plus control variates. Per-component leave-one-out on a 500-task audit set gets expensive as the number of components grows. With LiveBench-Math plus tau-bench-lite and one model family, a reviewer will say the multi-model, real-optimizer generality is not established.

Derive a single-lineage acceptance and stationary-load law, P_acc ~ Phi(s*sqrt(n)/sigma - z_gate), with L*(n, sigma, gate, u_add/u_del, DFE), and pre-register both the bloat prediction and the erosion prediction before running the large-n cells. Put the DFE per edit surface and out-of-sample prediction of final harness length on real optimizers (GEPA, ACE, and a Meta-Harness-style loop, using at least two open model families) up front as the headline. Treat the N_e gate as an ablation, compared at matched rollouts against Masked Erosion's paired and margin-aware gates, SHarP pruning, an RB-Prompt fixed length penalty, TRUST/SGM, and EvalAlloc CRN. Cite Masked Erosion first, and also cite the GP bloat literature (Langdon and Poli: introns, removal bias, 'fitness causes bloat'). Run the audit with grouped or stratified leave-one-out to keep within the $3k budget.
judges.reviewerQuote: The population-genetics framing is elegant, but Masked Erosion already did the gate-size sweep under a drift-vs-selection lens. I would raise my score if the paper led with the per-surface DFE and the two-sided bloat/erosion prediction tested out of sample on real optimizers, rather than an N_e gate that SHarP and RB-Prompt-style baselines may well match.

judges.strongest: The first measured distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of LLM proposer edits, split by edit surface (prompt, memory, tool, code), with neutral, deleterious and beneficial fractions and a gamma fit, would be a reusable artifact that nobody has published. It is cheap to get with local Qwen3 models and a fixed audit set, and the result is useful whichever way it comes out. A single acceptance law with two sides makes a sharp, counterintuitive prediction that can be falsified: raising n cuts slightly harmful bloat but speeds up erosion of cheap safeguards, and exactly-inert junk tracks the gate's tie rule rather than n. That gives the paper a clear headline figure.
judges.weakest: As stated, the theory does not fit the system. GEPA, ACE and Meta-Harness-style loops are elitist hill-climbers that follow a single lineage. They are not Wright-Fisher populations, so Kimura's P_fix(s, N_e) with 1/N_e neutral fixation does not apply. Masked Erosion's own no-op acceptance rates (0.40 greedy, 0.32 split-half, 0.013 paired) show that zero-cost junk is admitted at a rate set by the tie rule and stays flat in n. So the central claim is probably false for the components it focuses on. The 'import population genetics' pitch is already taken by Masked Erosion, and the intervention is largely covered by prior work: SHarP shows post-hoc 40% cuts, RB-Prompt and CoEvolve use length costs, and EvalAlloc uses CRN plus control variates. With gate n as the only knob, '1/N_e' collapses to n/σ², so the population-genetics label adds no explanatory power over a power analysis.
judges.mustFix: Drop Kimura and the gate-as-contribution framing. (1) Derive a stationary-load law for a single-lineage gate, P_acc(s) ≈ Φ(s√n/σ − z_gate) plus the tie-rule term for s = 0, and from it L*(n, σ, gate, u_add/u_del, DFE). (2) Make the per-surface DFE and out-of-sample prediction of final harness length on at least two real optimizers (GEPA, ACE) the headline. Use at least two model families.
